First, we analyzed the translational mobility of polymer crowder coils themselves as a function of the crower concentration. The FCS results showed that the translational mobility of crowder polymer coils decreased in a similar manner as rigid-body-like protein tracers (here, streptavidin) under the same crowding conditions. The translational diffusion on the FCS length scale (a few hundred nanometers) comes almost to rest for all macromolecules when the semidiluted regime is reached, approximately given by the overlap concentration for flexible polymers. Depending on the size of the polymer crowder coils or particles, this concentration is reached between 0.05 and 2.5 mM (from large to small crowders). A residual apparent slow diffusion visible in the FCS data is most probably an artifact caused by photobleaching effects. However, a fast local diffusion process of tracer molecules in the confined space, effectively built up by the polymer mesh, is still possible. According to the Huggins equation describing the bulk viscosity of concentrated polymer solutions, we obtain much higher viscosity values for larger crowding agents as compared to smaller ones at the same w/w% mass concentration. Therefore, we observed in the case of tracer diffusion that concentrated crowder solutions with larger crowding agents exhibit a much stronger deviation from the "macroscopic line" in D 0/D versus η/η0 plots as compared to smaller crowding agents. A direct look on the reduction of diffusion coefficients as a function of the crowder volume fraction revealed that PEG crowders cause the most pronounced reduction of the tracer diffusion. Furthermore, solutions with several crowder agents exhibit a tracer size-dependence of the diffusion reduction, which indicates a molecular sieving effect. This effect was also observed in the cytoplasm of cells and seems to be a general property of cellular crowding. With respect to absolute diffusion coefficients, we observe a reasonable agreement between measurements in cells and in synthetic crowder solutions for GFP. In the case of very slow diffusion, for example, for ribosomes in highly crowded environments, FCS measurements fail to deliver diffusion coefficients below ~1 μm2/s with the required accuracy. A more appropriate approach to study slow diffusion of biological macromolecules in crowded environments is given by single-particle tracking methods. In fact, a reliable knowledge about ribosome diffusion, but also about the diffusion of smaller molecules under the same crowding conditions, is of specific interest for elucidating the impact of macromolecular crowding on cellular processes, like, for example, the protein biosynthesis. In this respect, molecular sieving effects and the translational mobility of the 30S and 50S ribosomal subunits, the latter important for the 70S ribosome formation, are worth to be studied, for example, in cell-free protein synthesis assays. ,, Finally, we analyzed the impact of crowding on the performance of FRET-based glucose biosensors, equipped with FP derivatives as FRET pair. Although this sensor is designed to respond to ligand binding with a conformational change, it shows also pronounced crowding-induced conformational changes. In the case investigated here, glucose binding as well as the presence of macromolecular crowders lead to a structural compaction of the sensor construct, which both alter the FRET ratio. The crowder-induced sensor compaction only takes place if macromolecular crowders (PEG and Ficoll with a few up to a few tens of kDa mass) are used, whereas a compaction in the presence of small crowder agents (e.g.. glycerol) was not observed. Importantly, the sensor sensitivity (given by sufficiently large ΔR-values) is at least maintained under crowding conditions. However, the sensors would need an adapted calibration under equivalent crowding conditions, if employed under typical target conditions. The latter is challenging, specifically if such sensors are used intracellularily. In summary, we can state that synthetic polymer crowders can mimic already some properties of cellular crowding quite well, but it can be speculated that mixtures of multiple crowder agent components (also with more rigid crowder macromolecules, like double-stranded DNA or proteins) may give even more convincing results.

In conclusion, we analyzed the rotational motion of various proteins and proteinlike inclusions in membranes using extensive simulation data spanning different levels of protein concentrations from dilute membranes to realistically crowded ones. We found that the rotational diffusion rates of proteins decrease approximately exponentially with the increasing number of proteins with respect to that of membrane lipids. Only at very dilute conditions does rotational diffusion follow the SD model and scale as D rot ~ R -2. However, even at fairly dilute conditions compared to biologically relevant systems, a stronger D rot ~ R -3 scaling is observed. When the protein concentration is increased to levels characteristic for cellular membranes, the dependency of D rot on R becomes even stronger. Our synthetic 2-dimensional LJ simulations do not capture the scaling that is stronger than D rot ~ R -3, indicating that it arises due to specific protein-protein interactions. Therefore, our observations suggest that the SD model should be employed with care to estimate protein size or membrane properties, such as viscosity, in living cells or plasma-membrane-derived membranes. Moreover, since the reduced rate of rotational motion upon crowding may influence the detectability of interactions in NMR experiments, it might be better to consider the D rot ~ R -3 or a stronger scaling when estimating the detection limits in native membranes.

In the context of concentrated solutions, the size of the crowding agent influences the deviation from macroscopic diffusion behavior in several ways:

1.  **Effect on viscosity**: Larger crowding agents tend to exhibit higher viscosities at the same w/w% mass concentration compared to smaller agents, as described by the Huggins equation. This higher viscosity leads to a stronger deviation from the macroscopic diffusion behavior of tracer molecules.

2.  **Molecular sieving effect**: The size of the crowding agent can affect the diffusion of tracer molecules, leading to a molecular sieving effect. This means that smaller crowding agents may allow for faster diffusion of smaller tracer molecules, while larger agents may hinder their diffusion more significantly.

3.  **Confinement of the tracer molecules**: The size and shape of the crowding agents can create a confined space for the tracer molecules to diffuse. Smaller crowding agents may create a more open structure, allowing for faster diffusion, while larger agents may create a more compact structure, hindering diffusion.

Larger crowding agents may lead to a stronger dependence of rotational diffusion on the size of the particles.

5.  **Effect on energy transfer efficiency**: In the context of FRET-based sensors, larger crowding agents can lead to a more compact structure, increasing the energy transfer efficiency between the donor and acceptor molecules. In contrast, smaller agents may reduce the energy transfer efficiency due to reduced conformational fluctuations of the donor-acceptor pair.

In summary, the size of the crowding agent plays a crucial role in determining the deviation from macroscopic diffusion behavior in concentrated solutions. Larger agents tend to exhibit higher viscosities, create more compact structures, and influence the diffusion and rotational motion of tracer molecules more significantly.

dataset_item.question: How can high-performance liquid chromatography be used to purify compounds for photophysical measurements?
dataset_item.answer: High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) is an effective method for purifying compounds prior to photophysical measurements, ensuring high sample purity and minimizing interference during spectroscopic characterization. By employing a reverse-phase column, such as an XTerra RP18 (5 μm), and a mobile phase like acetonitrile at a controlled flow rate (e.g., 0.4 mL/min), HPLC can separate target molecules from impurities based on their chemical properties. Detection methods such as UV-vis spectroscopy or a photodiode array UV-vis detector are used to monitor and confirm the separation process. For instance, carbazole derivatives were purified using HPLC before analyzing their light-emitting properties, demonstrating its reliability for preparing high-purity samples essential for accurate photophysical measurements.

dataset_item.question: Why is the syn reaction path favored over the anti reaction path in terms of Gibbs enthalpy for aldehydes with alkyl, vinyl, or aromatic substituents?
dataset_item.answer: The *syn* reaction path is favored over the *anti* reaction path for aldehydes with alkyl, vinyl, or aromatic substituents due to the lower Gibbs enthalpy barrier associated with the *syn* transition state (Tc) compared to the *anti* transition state (Tb). This energetic preference arises from the greater stability of Tc, which is attributed to the concerted migration of the trimethylsilyl (SiMe₃) group attached to Oα. Density Functional Theory (DFT) calculations confirm that Tc is lower in energy, making the *syn* pathway kinetically favored. Additionally, the *syn* product (3 *syn*) is thermodynamically more stable than the *anti* product (3 *anti*), further reinforcing the energetic advantage of the *syn* route for all substituents studied. Thus, both the transition state and product stability collectively favor the *syn* reaction path over the *anti* pathway.

inference_contexts: Theoretical investigations using density functional theory with the M06-2X functional have been performed to unravel the concerted mechanism of the uncatalyzed Mukaiyama aldol reaction between C,O,O-tris (trimethylsilyl) ketene acetal 1 and aldehydes 2 bearing alkyl, vinyl, or aromatic substituents. These DFT calculations show that (i) the 3 syn product is both the kinetic and the thermodynamic product and that (ii) the diastereoselectivity of the uncatalyzed reaction is larger than observed for the reaction catalyzed by HgI2 and it is inverted with respect to the latter. These calculations have substantiated the fact that solvents with larger dielectric constants increase the activation barrier but reduce the diastereoselectivity. They have also confirmed the preference for the concerted reaction over the stepwise reactions as well as the key role of the OSiMe3 group in geminal on lowering the activation barrier and increasing the energy of reaction. Moreover, the study of the concerted mechanism highlights four types of cyclic transition states (Ta, Tb, Tc, Td). The Tb conformation is the most stable pro-anti transition state whereas Tc is a most stable pro-syn. Both Tb and Tc correspond to the migration of the SiMe3 group attached to Oα, i.e.. on the opposite side to the SiMe3 substituent. Then, comparison between Tb and Tc as well as between their corresponding product, 3 anti and 3 syn, leads to conclude that, for all substituents, the syn reaction path is located at lower energy (Gibbs enthalpy) than the anti reaction path.

A single-exponential down model was used to approximate the collisional energy transfer with ⟨ΔE⟩down of 250 cm-1. The collision frequencies were estimated by the method of Gilbert and Smith, and the tunneling correction factors were included in the microcanonical rates by the method of Miller.

The determination of the energy landscape and transition-state energy, configuration, and barriers were performed using the climbing image nudged elastic band method (CI-NEB) as implemented in the USPEX code v10.3. , The force convergence criterion for each image on the reaction path was set to 2 × 10-3 eV/Å, and the steepest descendent algorithm was chosen for the reaction path optimization.

To obtain the minimum energy path (V mep) and compute the chemical kinetic properties, the calculations were performed with the M06-2X/maTZ methodology and the algorithm proposed by Page and McIver as implemented in the Gaussrate program. Next, the reaction path surfaces were improved with the electronic properties (Δ E , V ⧧, Δ E RW, and Δ E PW) obtained from the CCSD (T)/aTZ//M06-2X/maTZ calculations. This approach is known as dual-level methodology.

dataset_item.question: What are the specific photochemical pathways and mechanisms that govern the conversion of trans-BIPSB and 9-cis-BIPSB into other isomeric forms under near-UV light?
dataset_item.answer: Under near-UV light (320–400 nm), *trans*-BIPSB undergoes sequential photochemical transformations, initially isomerizing to *7-cis*-BIPSB and subsequently cyclizing into a photostable bicyclic structure that becomes inert to further visible and near-UV irradiation. In contrast, *9-cis*-BIPSB undergoes photoisomerization to form *7,9-di-cis*-BIPSB but cannot cyclize due to steric hindrance. Additionally, the *γ*-ionone isomer is formed from *trans*-BIPSB via a [1-5] sigmatropic hydrogen atom shift. This isomer is photochemically inactive under near-UV and visible light due to disrupted conjugation, which prevents further light-induced transformations. These pathways demonstrate the critical roles of geometric isomerism, steric constraints, and conjugation in determining the photochemical behavior of BIPSB isomers.

dataset_item.question: How do specific mole fractions influence solvation time and structural transitions in tert-butyl alcohol-water and ethanol-water binary mixtures?
dataset_item.answer:
Specific mole fractions play a critical role in influencing solvation time and structural transitions in tert-butyl alcohol (TBA)-water and ethanol-water binary mixtures. In TBA-water mixtures, slowed solvation is observed at mole fractions \(X_T = 0.09-0.15\) and \(X_T = 0.40-0.46\). The increase in solvation time at \(X_T = 0.40-0.46\) is attributed to higher shear viscosity, while at \(X_T = 0.09-0.15\), it results from a structural transition from a water-like tetrahedral network to an alcohol-like zigzag structure. Interestingly, faster solvation occurs at \(X_T = 0.02-0.03\), and anomalous behavior is noted around \(X_T = 0.04\), likely tied to hindered molecular rotation of the probe.

In ethanol-water mixtures, solvation time increases at mole fractions \(X_E = 0.06-0.08\) and \(X_E = 0.20-0.25\). Similar to TBA-water mixtures, the slower solvation at higher ethanol fractions (\(X_E = 0.20-0.25\)) is linked to increased viscosity, while at lower fractions (\(X_E = 0.06-0.08\)), the structural transition from a tetrahedral water network to an alcohol-like arrangement governs solvation dynamics. Temperature-dependent studies further reveal that alcohol aggregation intensifies with rising temperature, consistent with stick boundary behavior in solute-solvent coupling.

Overall, solvation dynamics in both mixtures are governed by complex interactions involving structural rearrangements, viscosity effects, and probe molecule behavior at specific mole fractions.

dataset_item.question: What is the role of surfactants in the dye mixture used for optical acidity measurement in ice cores?
dataset_item.answer: Surfactants, specifically Brij L23, are incorporated into the dye mixture used for optical acidity measurements in ice cores to serve two critical functions. First, they reduce surface tension, facilitating the removal of air bubbles from the absorption cell. This ensures consistent light intensity measurements and enhances the accuracy of pH detection. Second, surfactants may influence air-water CO₂ exchange dynamics, potentially mitigating temperature-dependent CO₂ effects on pH measurements. However, studies indicate that the sealed system used for these measurements is not significantly affected by ambient CO₂. The dye mixture comprises bromophenol blue and chlorophenol red dissolved in Milli-Q water, with Brij L23 added at 100 μL (30% w/w) to optimize the analytical process.

### 1. Summary of the Purpose:
The paper aims to introduce and validate a new optical method for determining acidity in ice cores using pH-indicator dyes (bromophenol blue and chlorophenol red). This method is simpler and faster than existing techniques, with no need for CO₂ equilibration, and is tested on ice cores from Greenland and Antarctica. The study compares the results with standard methods (e.g., electrical conductivity and ion chromatography) and explores correlations between acidity and environmental events, such as volcanic eruptions and marine influences.

### 2. Classification of Purpose:

Optimal dye concentration was found with a sample flow rate of 0.9 mL/min and 0.15 mL/min of dye mixture (see Supporting Information Figure S1). The dye mixture is made by dissolving 0.025 g of bromophenol blue and 0.025 g of chlorophenol red in 500 mL of Milli-Q water (Millipore A10 Advantage, 18.2 MΩ.cm) and adding 100 μL Brij L23 (30%w/w). The sample and dye are mixed in a 1 m long mixing coil kept in a 65 °C heat bath, after which the mixture passes through a 6 cm-long Accurel (PP S6/2, Membrana GmbH, Germany) gas permeable membrane to allow the removal of excess air bubbles created during the heating. dataset_item.question: How does vibrational excitation of methane and oxygen influence dissociative adsorption reactions and Eley-Rideal reactions in plasma-catalytic partial oxidation on platinum surfaces?
dataset_item.answer: Vibrational excitation of methane (CH4) and oxygen (O2) significantly influences dissociative adsorption reactions and Eley-Rideal reactions in plasma-catalytic partial oxidation on platinum (Pt(111)) surfaces. Microkinetic modeling reveals that vibrational energy lowers the enthalpy barriers for these reactions by reducing their activation energies, leading to enhanced reaction rates. Specifically, vibrational excitation promotes the dissociative adsorption of CH4 and O2 on the platinum surface, as well as Eley-Rideal reactions between gaseous CH4 and surface-bound hydroxyl (OH*) or oxygen (O*) intermediates. These modifications improve the efficiency of plasma-catalytic partial oxidation processes, favoring the formation of valuable oxygenates such as methanol and formic acid. Additionally, the transition state for these processes is assumed to lose all translational entropy, further influencing reaction kinetics. By accounting for vibrational energy effects, this approach provides deeper insights into the reaction pathways and the role of plasma-catalysis in optimizing partial oxidation reactions on Pt surfaces.

The model shows that vibrational excitation of CH4 and O2 can enhance the rates of dissociative adsorption and Eley-Rideal reactions, leading to an increase in the conversion of methane.

dataset_item.question: How does the degree of silicification influence the binding energy between silicon compounds and cadmium ions?
dataset_item.answer:
The degree of silicification significantly influences the binding energy between silicon compounds and cadmium ions (Cd(II)) by modifying the structural and chemical composition of the silicon surface. Molecular dynamics simulations were employed to study this relationship, with varying degrees of silicification modeled by adjusting the molar ratio of SiO₂ to Si(OH)₄ while maintaining a consistent number of silicon atoms (e.g., 288 atoms). Fully silicified surfaces (100% SiO₂) were represented by hydroxylated cristobalite as a proxy for amorphous silica, while lower silicification levels (75%, 50%, 25%) included increasing proportions of Si(OH)₄.

Binding energy was calculated using the formula: 
E_bin = E_Si+Cd(II) - (E_Si + E_Cd(II)),  
where E_Si+Cd(II) represents the total energy of the system including silicon compounds and cadmium ions, E_Si is the energy of silicon compounds, and E_Cd(II) is the energy of cadmium ions.

Results showed a direct correlation between the degree of silicification and binding energy. Higher silicification (increased SiO₂ content) enhanced the interaction strength between Cd(II) and silicon surfaces due to increased coordination with surface silanol groups on solid SiO₂. In contrast, lower silicification (higher Si(OH)₄ content) reduced binding energy, as Cd(II) interacted more weakly with dissolved silicic acid than with solid silica surfaces. The study utilized periodic boundary conditions and the universal force field to ensure accurate simulation of the interactions, confirming that amorphous silica surfaces exhibit the strongest binding affinity for Cd(II) ions under fully silicified conditions.

dataset_item.question: How does N-oxidation affect molecular stability and electronic properties of N-rich heteroaromatic derivatives?
dataset_item.answer:
N-oxidation generally reduces molecular stability in N-rich heteroaromatic derivatives by elongating vicinal bonds, lowering aromaticity (as confirmed by NICS analysis), and narrowing the HOMO-LUMO gap, which increases photochemical reactivity and sensitivity. This destabilization is attributed to enhanced electron repulsion and reduced conjugation. However, in select cases, such as 1,2,3,4-tetrazine-1,3-dioxide and tetrazine tri-oxides (TTTO), N-oxidation promotes stabilization by enhancing σ-π separation, reducing lone-pair repulsion, and enabling alternating charge stabilization. This stabilization is more pronounced in systems with efficient charge separation.

Additionally, N-oxidation increases the positive molecular electrostatic potential (MEP), especially over N-H bonds, which may enhance compound sensitivity. The N+-O− bonds formed during oxidation contribute to the reactivity and sensitivity of the molecule. Despite the destabilizing trends, oxidation reactions using oxidizers like N₂O and H₂O₂ are thermodynamically favorable and kinetically feasible, with barriers typically ranging between 22.1–42.7 kcal/mol. Among analyzed N-oxides, 19 candidates were identified as stable high-energy materials, highlighting the potential for selective stabilization in specific systems.

1.  **Weakening of molecular stability**: The introduction of an N-oxide group can stretch vicinal bonds on the conjugated ring, reducing molecular aromaticity and stability.
2.  **Narrowing of HOMO-LUMO gap**: N-oxidation can decrease the energy gap between the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) and the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO), potentially increasing photochemical reactivity.
3.  **Increased charge separation**: The introduction of an N-oxide group can facilitate charge separation, contributing to ring stabilization in some cases, such as 1,2,3,4-tetrazine-1,3-dioxide and TTTO.
4.  **Enhanced positive MEPs**: N+-O- bonds can increase the positive molecular electrostatic potential (MEP) over N-H bonds in azole rings and the center of azine rings, potentially increasing sensitivity to reagents.
5.  **Thermodynamically spontaneous oxidation**: N-oxidation reactions using N2O and H2O2 as oxidizers are thermodynamically spontaneous and kinetically feasible, with energy barriers ranging from 22.1 to 42.7 kcal/mol.
6.  **Ring-chain isomerization**: N-rich systems, such as 1,2,3,4-tetrazine-1-oxide, may undergo ring-chain isomerization due to the introduction of the N-oxide group.
7.  **Stabilization strategy**: The introduction of N+-O- bonds does not appear to be an effective stabilization strategy, as it can lead to a decrease in molecular stability.

Overall, N-oxidation can have both positive and negative effects on the molecular stability and electronic properties of N-rich heteroaromatic derivatives, depending on the specific system and the nature of the N-oxide group introduced.

dataset_item.question: How do computational methods such as CC2 and time-dependent DFT, using different exchange-correlation functionals, compare in predicting band shapes and excitation energies for one-photon absorption spectra of bis (BF2) core complexes?
dataset_item.answer:
Computational methods such as CC2 and time-dependent density functional theory (TD-DFT) were compared for predicting the one-photon absorption spectra of bis(BF₂) core complexes. Among the exchange-correlation functionals employed in TD-DFT, CAM-B3LYP, BHandHLYP, and M06-HF demonstrated superior performance in reproducing the experimental band shape of the intense one-photon allowed 1¹A_g → 1¹B_u transition. In contrast, B3LYP and PBE0 performed poorly in predicting band shapes. However, the vertical excitation energies predicted by CAM-B3LYP, BHandHLYP, and M06-HF deviated significantly from CC2 results, with differences ranging from 0.57–1.0 eV, highlighting a trade-off between accuracy in band shape prediction and excitation energy estimation. 

Herzberg-Teller effects were found to have minimal influence on vibrational fine structure, while non-Condon effects played a significant role in two-photon transitions. For modeling environmental broadening effects, polarizable embedding CC2 and state-specific PCM methods provided the best agreement with experimental data, further improving the accuracy of spectral predictions. Overall, CC2 showed better consistency in predicting experimental band shapes and excitation energies compared to TD-DFT.
dataset_item.topic:
### 1. **Summary of the Purpose**
The paper aims to computationally investigate the vibrationally resolved one- and two-photon absorption spectra of bis (BF2) core complexes, both in vacuum and in solution. It focuses on understanding the effects of inhomogeneous broadening and non-Condon effects on the spectral band shapes. Advanced computational methods, including polarizable embedding (PE), time-dependent DFT, coupled cluster CC2, and polarizable continuum models (PCM), are applied to simulate and analyze spectral features. The study evaluates the accuracy of different methods for modeling environmental broadening and explores the mechanisms of electronic excitation in two-photon transitions.

---

### 2. **Classification of Purpose**
- The purpose of the paper emphasizes **"<method>"**, as it focuses on the development, application, and comparison of computational methodologies for accurately simulating vibrationally resolved absorption spectra.

---

### 3. **Relevant Research Questions**
- How accurately can computational methods such as CC2, time-dependent DFT, and PCM simulate the inhomogeneous broadening in absorption spectra of bis (BF2) complexes?
- What are the relative contributions of non-Condon effects to the band shapes of one- and two-photon transitions in bis (BF2) complexes?
- How does the choice of environmental modeling approach (e.g., polarizable embedding vs. state-specific PCM) affect the accuracy of spectral simulations?
- What are the key optical channels involved in two-photon electronic excitations, and how do intermediate states (e.g., 11B u) influence these transitions?
- How do the findings inform general modeling strategies for vibrationally resolved band shapes in complex molecular systems?

inference_contexts: This paper is motivated by the versatility and applicability of boron-dipyrromethene (BODIPY) complexes and other BF2-carrying molecules as commonly used fluorophores. To unravel what is required to capture their optical spectra, we carried out a systematic computational study of vibrationally resolved one- and two-photon absorption spectra of the recently synthesized bis (BF2) core complex and its unmethylated derivative in vacuum and in solution (in ACN and DCM solvents). The one-photon absorption spectra were simulated using the CC2 method as well as by means of the density functional theory. In the latter case, several exchange-correlation functionals were employed, including B3LYP, PBE0, CAM-B3LYP, BHandHLYP, and M06-HF. It is demonstrated that the latter three functionals are much more successful than B3LYP or PBE0 in predicting the band shape corresponding to the intense one-photon allowed 11A g → 11B u transition. In general, a fair agreement between the simulated and experimental band shapes for 11A g → 11B u transition has been found, while the vertical excitation energies predicted by CAM-B3LYP, BHandHLYP, and M06-HF largely deviate from the CC2 result with a difference span of 0.57-1.0 eV. We have also shown that Herzberg-Teller contributions have only minor influence on the vibrational fine structure of the 11A g → 11B u band. On the other hand, non-Condon effects play a major role in the case of two-photon allowed 11A g → 21A g transition for the bis (BF2) core complex. A generalized few-level model has also been employed to analyze the mechanism of the electronic two-photon 11A g → 21A g excitation. It has been found that the most important optical channel involves the 11B u excited state. This is a practical hint for studies aiming at maximizing the two-photon absorption cross section for derivatives of bis (BF2) core complex.

The nonempirical estimation of inhomogeneous broadening is a key ingredient of computational protocols employed for simulations of one- and two-photon absorption spectra in solution. For this purpose, and following our earlier study, we have employed a polarizable embedding approach combined with TD-DFT and CC2 methods. Moreover, the inhomogeneous broadening has also been determined based on the Marcus theory employing linear response-PCM, corrected linear response PCM, as well as state-specific PCM methods. A comparison with experimental data reveals that the polarizable embedding CC2 and SS-PCM are the most successful approaches for the description of environmental effects, thus becoming a solid foundation for purely ab initio simulations of multiphoton vibronic spectra of molecules in solution. We believe that the current study, applied to an important chromophore system, illustrates what can be accomplished, as well as what is required, by current state-of-the-art simulations of optical spectra, both with respect to excitation energies and band shapes.

We present the vertical and adiabatic excitation energies to the low-lying excited states, namely, 2Ag -, 1Bu +, and 1Bu -, for polyenes containing 8-13 conjugated double bonds. With the computational protocol used, we achieved an accuracy within 2000 cm-1 for the 2Ag - state and within 6000 cm-1 for the 1Bu - state, together with the expected MRPT negative error of 4000 cm-1 for the 1Bu - state for the longest polyene, 13-ene, studied. For smaller polyenes, the error estimates are almost twice as better in the case of the two lowest excited states (2Ag - and 1Bu +) and slightly better in the case of 1Bu - than those for 13-ene. The obtained relative energies of the excited states do not contradict the recently obtained excitation energies for natural carotenoids, while the adiabatic energy of 2Ag - is considerably lower due to a better geometry optimization procedure. Vibronic profiles for absorption spectra from the ground state to the excited states were calculated from first principles together with the transient absorption spectra from the 2Ag - to the 1Bu + state. Based on the latter, the two different experimental assignments for the 0 → 0 energy reported previously are compared. It is demonstrated that the data presented here matches better the study by Wang et al.. predicting rather high energies for 2Ag -.

Ab initio calculations were carried out with the TURBOMOLE program package, making use of the resolution-of-the-identity (RI) approximation to evaluate the electron-repulsion integrals. Ground state (S0) equilibrium geometries of protonated species were optimized at the MP2 (second order Møller-Plesset perturbation) level of theory using the cc-pVDZ (correlation-consistent polarized valence double-zeta) basis set. Vertical excitation energies, oscillator strengths, and equilibrium geometries of the lowest excited singlet states were computed at the CC2 (second-order approximate coupled cluster) level, because standard time-dependent DFT (density functional theory) is well-known to produce substantial errors in representing charge transfer (CT) excited states. Moreover, we have chosen the RI-CC2 method because it proved useful in describing the electronic transitions of similar aromatic ions with nitrogen functional groups. , In all the calculations the starting geometries had Cs symmetry and were constrained to distinguish between π or σ orbitals and A′ or A″ excited states. In the case of the benzenediazonium ion fragment, adiabatic excitation energies were calculated in addition to the vertical excitation values. For doing this, the energies of the ground and the first two excited states were computed for the optimized S1(A′) and S2(A′) excited state geometries, in Cs symmetry. Additional excited state optimizations were performed for this system and protonated azobenzene, relaxing the condition of maintaining Cs symmetry and allowing nonplanar geometries.

We report the excitation wavelength dependence of the FSRS spectrum for the T1 state of PT and compare the trends we observe to simulated on- and off-resonance Raman spectra using several theoretical approaches. The experimental results provide a rigorous benchmark for the accuracy of the computational techniques, whereas the computational results highlight the difficulties of interpreting FSRS spectra involving more than one resonant or nearly resonant electronic transition. These results also point to important limitations of the FC and FCHT approaches for the calculation of resonance Raman spectra in the presence of broad, overlapping transitions. The more densely packed manifold of the high-lying electronic states makes it difficult to extrapolate the PES from the excited-state minimum to the Franck-Condon geometry using the harmonic approximation.

The study compares the performance of computational methods, specifically CC2 and time-dependent DFT (TD-DFT) using different exchange-correlation functionals, in predicting the one-photon absorption spectra of bis(BF2) core complexes. Here's a summary of the key findings:

**Methods and Functionals:**

1. **CC2 (Coupled Cluster with Singles and Doubles) method:** A high-level ab initio method that is well-suited for predicting excited state properties, including excitation energies and band shapes.
2. **TD-DFT (Time-Dependent Density Functional Theory):** A popular method for calculating excited state properties, but often prone to errors in charge transfer excited states.
3. **Exchange-Correlation Functionals:** Several functionals were employed, including B3LYP, PBE0, CAM-B3LYP, BHandHLYP, and M06-HF.

**Results:**

1. **One-Photon Absorption Spectra:**
	* CC2 method: Predicted the band shape and excitation energy of the 11A g → 11B u transition with high accuracy.
	* TD-DFT with CAM-B3LYP, BHandHLYP, and M06-HF functionals: Predicted the band shape with good accuracy but deviated from the CC2 result by 0.57-1.0 eV in excitation energy.
	* B3LYP and PBE0 functionals performed poorly in predicting the band shape.
2. **Herzberg-Teller Contributions:** Found to have minor influence on the vibrational fine structure of the 11A g → 11B u band.
3. **Non-Condon Effects:** Played a major role in the two-photon allowed 11A g → 21A g transition.
4. **Two-Photon Absorption Spectra:** A generalized few-level model was used to analyze the mechanism of the electronic two-photon 11A g → 21A g excitation, and the most important optical channel involved the 11B u excited state.
5. **Inhomogeneous Broadening:** Estimated using polarizable embedding approaches (CC2 and SS-PCM) and linear response-PCM methods, with polarizable embedding CC2 and SS-PCM being the most successful approaches.

**Conclusion:**

* The study highlights the importance of choosing the right method and functional for predicting one-photon absorption spectra of bis(BF2) core complexes.
* CC2 method is recommended for predicting band shapes and excitation energies.
* TD-DFT with CAM-B3LYP, BHandHLYP, and M06-HF functionals can be used for predicting band shapes, but may require further refinement.
* Non-Condon effects play a crucial role in two-photon absorption spectra.
* Inhomogeneous broadening can be estimated using polarizable embedding approaches and linear response-PCM methods.

dataset_item.question: What are the rate constants and their pressure dependencies for reactions involving hydrogen atom and oxygen molecule in supercritical CO2 environments?
dataset_item.answer:
The rate constants and their pressure dependencies for reactions involving hydrogen atom and oxygen molecule in supercritical CO₂ environments have been studied under high-pressure conditions (100–400 atm). 

For the reaction **H + O₂ ⇌ HO + O (R1)**, the rate constant is pressure-independent within the specified pressure range and is significantly lower—two orders of magnitude—than the rate constant at ambient pressure. At 300 atm, the rate constant for R1 is given as:  
\[
k_{\text{R1}} = 4.23 \times 10^{-7} \, T^{-0.73} \exp\left(-\frac{21,855.2 \, \text{cal/mol}}{RT}\right) \, \text{cm}^3/\text{molecule/s}.
\]

For the reaction **H + O₂ ⇌ HO₂ (R2)**, the rate constant exhibits pressure dependence, increasing with pressure within the same range. At 300 atm, the rate constant for R2 is:  
\[
k_{\text{R2}} = 5.22 \times 10^{-2} \, T^{-2.86} \exp\left(-\frac{7,247.4 \, \text{cal/mol}}{RT}\right) \, \text{cm}^3/\text{molecule/s}.
\]

These findings were derived using quantum chemical calculations, transition state theory, and molecular dynamics simulations, offering valuable insights into the kinetics of hydrogen oxidation in high-pressure supercritical CO₂ environments.

### 1. Summary of the Paper's Purpose:
The paper aims to investigate the chemical kinetics of two key reactions, **H + O2 ⇌ HO + O** and **H + O2 ⇌ HO2**, which are critical in hydrogen and hydrocarbon oxidation mechanisms under high-pressure, supercritical CO2 (sCO2) environments relevant to advanced energy technologies such as oxy-combustion and the Allam cycle. The study combines quantum transition state theory, classical molecular dynamics simulations, and multistate empirical valence bonding methods to account for environmental effects. Reaction rates are quantified under varying temperatures (1000–2000 K) and pressures (100–400 atm), providing key insights into pressure-dependence and temperature scaling.

---

### 2. Purpose Classification:
**<Result>**
The primary focus of the paper is on obtaining specific reaction rate data and understanding how these rates depend on pressure and temperature in an sCO2 environment. While methods are discussed, the emphasis is on the results and their implications for energy technologies.

---

### 3. Relevant Research Questions:
- How do environmental factors, such as high pressure and supercritical CO2 conditions, affect the chemical kinetics of hydrogen and oxygen reactions?
- What are the reaction rate constants for **H + O2 ⇌ HO + O** and **H + O2 ⇌ HO2** under high-pressure and high-temperature sCO2 environments?
- How do pressure and temperature influence the reaction mechanisms and rates of these oxidation reactions?
- Can the reaction rate expressions derived from this study be generalized for other combustion systems in supercritical CO2 environments?
- What role does the multistate empirical valence bonding method play in accurately modeling the environmental effects on these reaction systems? 
- How do the derived reaction rate expressions contribute to the optimization of advanced energy technologies like the Allam cycle?

inference_contexts: We evaluated the rate constants for the reactions R1 and R2 between a hydrogen atom and an oxygen molecule in a supercritical CO2 environment and its Arrhenius parameters. These reaction are among the most important reactions in hydrocarbon combustion mechanism. To accurately evaluate k of these reactions, high-level quantum chemical calculations were performed at the CCSD (T)/aug-cc-pVQZ//CCSD/cc-pVDZ theory level to calculate the rate constant of R2 in the gas phase by TST first. Classical MD simulations were performed to study the dynamics of chemical reactions with explicit CO2 molecules included in conjunction with the MS-EVB method to reproduce potential energy of free radical reactions. TST was applied to calculate k of R2, followed by the RRKM method to calculate k of R1 and R2 at high pressures from 100 to 400 atm. The rate constant of reaction R1 was found to be pressure-independent between 100 and 400 atm in bimolecular reaction with only one product and is two orders of magnitude lower than that at ambient pressure. The rate constant of reaction R1 at 300 atm was found to be 4.23 × 10-7 T-0.73 exp (-21 855.2 cal/mol/RT) cm3/molecule/s. The rate constant of reaction R2 demonstrates pressure-dependence between 100 and 400 atm and increases with the pressure. The rate constant of reaction R2 at 300 atm was found to be 5.22 × 10-2 T-2.86 exp (-7247.4 cal/mol/RT) cm3/molecule/s.

We reported free energy profiles and rate constants predicted by the method of boxed molecular dynamics in hybrid quantum-classical theory level (QM/MM). Both forward steps and , reverse processes R2r and R3r, as well as the total transformation of , were investigated under different temperatures and pressures. The results obtained make it possible to draw the following generalizations: 1 The temperature dependences of rate constants for the forward reaction and and reverse processes R2r and R3r, as well as the gross reaction k 1, are close to Arrhenius. The calculated numerical parameters of the extended Arrhenius equation are presented in Tables , , , , and . 2 With increasing CO2 pressure in the system, rate constant for the reaction rises in the pressure range from 0.3 to 100 atm and almost does not depend on pressure at higher values of P. 3 An analogous growth of the rate constants with increasing total pressure is observed for the elementary processes , R2r, and . However, for the R3r process, there is an opposite trend: decrease in the rate constant with increasing P, also with access to the plateau in the region of high pressures. Presumably, this effect is due to solvation effects involving OH radicals. 4 Comparison of values of the rate constants with previous experimental data indicates the need to take into account the pressure in system when calculating the parameters of the extended Arrhenius equation. The effect of CO2 on the growth of reaction rate constants - allows us to assume that the buffer gases based on it are potentially effective colliders for combustion reaction.

The computation of the forward rate constants confirmed that reactions involving edge type A are faster than others. It was noted that generally having the σ-radical on the five-member ring resulted in faster kinetics than when the σ-radical was on the six-member ring. At flame temperatures of 1400-2000 K, the forward rate constants were generally of the order of 108 to 1012 cm3mol-1 s-1. Notably, the rate constants between PAHs with edge type A and edge type D and edge type A and edge type B were seen to be as large or even larger than for that between two of edge type A. It was also seen that the rate constant for the reaction between A1 and A2 was substantially faster than that between A1 and A1 or A2 and A2. The reaction between two localized π-radicals on rim five-member rings was seen to be notably faster at temperatures below 1000 K but then declines and is one of the slowest reactions at 2000 K. Reactions involving combinations of edge types B, C, D, and E were generally seen to be slower in comparison. Generally, all computed rate constants are unlikely to be high enough to result in substantial enough fluxes for processes such as soot formation on their own, as the higher rate constants involve reactions between two radical PAHs that are expected to be in lower concentrations. This is also true for suggestions involving cross-links on five-member rings and delocalized π-radical PAHs.

Although intermolecular distances for CO2 were found to be slightly larger than those in the Monte Carlo calculations, the distances from CPMD were found to be in good agreement with Saharay and Balasubramanian. It shows that the classical force field can generate a more structured fluid than CPMD simulations with the BLYP functional. The radial distribution functions of CO2 around thiophene in the supercritical state show the higher correlation along the direction of cooperative S C and C-H O hydrogen bonding interaction. Through the analysis of angular-radial distribution functions, a mutually parallel arrangement between thiophene plane and CO2 molecules is favored at short distances. The SDFs results indicate that the thiophene molecule prefers to be located near the axis of CO2 molecule. However, there is preference for CO2 molecules to be located near the sulfur atom of the thiophene molecule, indicating that it can help to form a cooperative C-H O hydrogen bond in the mixture. In addition, the decay of orientational correlations for 318.15 K shows slower relaxation compared to that of 298.15 K for first and second rank correlations. The vibrations of CO2 and thiophene molecules have been examined through an analysis of the VACFs of the atoms. The C-H stretching modes of thiophene in the isolated configuration are less red-shifted and have a much narrower frequency range than that in the mixtures. Through the comparison of the calculated C-H stretching positions with the available experimental data, the spectral ranges obtained using CPMD methodologies are in good agreement with the experimental data.

As demonstrated in this Review, tremendous advances have been made in the gold-catalyzed nitrene-transfer reactions and carbene-transfer reactions involving oxygen atom transfer over the past few decades. Through treatment of readily available alkynes with nitrene-transfer reagents and oxygen atom-transfer reagents in the presence of gold catalysts, α-imino gold carbene species and α-oxo gold carbene species could be generated as key intermediates, respectively, which are able to undergo various siginificant transformations including X-H insertion, 1,2-migration, formal annulation, cyclopropanation, electrocyclization, ylide rearrangement, and so on, thus significantly enriching gold carbene chemistry. These protocols provide powerful and efficient methods for the rapid assembly of valuable natural or non-natural products. It is notable that α-imino gold carbene species in gold-catalyzed nitrene-transfer reactions were rarely produced from the corresponding α-imino diazo compounds by metal-catalyzed dediazotizations of diazo compounds. Meanwhile, α-oxo gold carbene species could be generated efficiently from the corresponding α-oxo diazo compounds, but the use of not easily accessible and potentially explosive diazo compounds severely limits its further synthetic applications. Therefore, gold-catalyzed nitrene- and carbene-transfer reactions based on alkynes provide much more convenient and safer operations in gold carbene chemistry. Despite these achievements, there is still room for further exploration: (a) There is no direct structural evidence to indicate the presence of such α-imino and α-oxo gold carbene species because they are neither isolated nor spectroscopically detected or characterized. (b) It is difficult to distinguish whether gold carbene intermediates have been experienced, and noncarbene pathways are also reasonable in some specific cases. (c) Catalytic asymmetric versions based on gold-catalyzed nitrene-transfer and carbene-transfer reactions involving oxygen atom transfer have been rarely demonstrated and are always challenging in gold catalysis. (d) Low atom economy still exists, especially in this type of gold-catalyzed carbene-transfer reaction; thus, the development of more atom-economic and environmentally friendly nitrene- and oxygen-transfer reagents remains highly desirable. Therefore, we anticipate that studies of gold-catalyzed nitrene-transfer and carbene-transfer reactions involving oxygen atom transfer will attract more interest by chemists to contribute to the development of this research field.

dataset_item.question: What are the single-step quantum yields for cyclization reactions of 1,2-bis (2-methyl-3-benzothienyl) perfluorocyclopentene, 1,2-bis (2-hexyl-3-benzothienyl) perfluorocyclopentene, and 1,2-bis (2-isopropyl-3-benzothienyl) perfluorocyclopentene via their excited triplet states?
dataset_item.answer: The single-step quantum yields for the cyclization reactions of 1,2-bis(2-methyl-3-benzothienyl)perfluorocyclopentene, 1,2-bis(2-hexyl-3-benzothienyl)perfluorocyclopentene, and 1,2-bis(2-isopropyl-3-benzothienyl)perfluorocyclopentene via their excited triplet states are 0.34, 0.53, and 0.65, respectively. These values were determined using triplet sensitization with sensitizers possessing energies above ~200 kJ mol⁻¹. The yields are comparable to or significantly higher than those observed from the singlet excited states, demonstrating the efficiency of triplet-sensitized cyclization. This approach provides an effective alternative to visible-light-initiated reactions, offering enhanced control for diarylethene-based functional devices.
dataset_item.topic:
### 1. **Summary of the Purpose of the Paper**  
The paper investigates the cyclization reactions of three diarylethene derivatives (BT, BTHex, and BTiPr) through their excited triplet states. The study utilizes steady-state and nanosecond transient absorption spectroscopy to characterize these reactions. By employing energy transfer from photoexcited triplet states of sensitizers (e.g., xanthone, phenanthrene, and pyrene), the research determines the single-step quantum yields of the cyclization reactions and estimates the triplet energies of the derivatives.

---

### 2. **Classification of Purpose**  
**<Result>**  
The study primarily focuses on reporting the quantum yields and triplet energy values of the cyclization reactions, making it result-oriented.

---

### 3. **Research Questions**  
- What are the quantum yields of cyclization reactions for the three diarylethene derivatives in their excited triplet states?  
- How do the structural differences (e.g., methyl, hexyl, and isopropyl substituents) in the diarylethene derivatives influence their quantum yields and triplet energies?  
- What are the triplet energy levels of BT, BTHex, and BTiPr, and how do these levels relate to their photochemical reactivity?  
- How do different sensitizers (xanthone, phenanthrene, and pyrene) facilitate energy transfer to generate the excited triplet states of these derivatives?  
- What are the implications of the observed quantum yields and triplet energies for the design of photoresponsive materials or molecular switches?

inference_contexts: Cyclization reactions of naked diarylethene via its excited triplet state have not been reported, and basic data for the excited triplet state of diarylethene derivatives are completely lacking. Here, we studied the cyclization of three diarylethene derivatives, 1,2-bis (2-methyl-3-benzothienyl) perfluorocyclopentene, 1,2-bis (2-hexyl-3-benzothienyl) perfluorocyclopentene, and 1,2-bis (2-isopropyl-3-benzothienyl) perfluorocyclopentene with various triplet sensitizers. Upon irradiation of a sensitizer with a triplet energy larger than ca. 200 kJ mol-1, cyclization reactions of three derivatives occurred via the excited triplet states. Single-step quantum yields for the cyclization reactions of three derivatives were as large as 0.34, 0.53, and 0.65, respectively. These values are either almost equal to or much higher than the corresponding quantum yields from the excited singlet state. Our results indicate that the efficiency of the cyclization reactions of diarylethene derivatives can be controlled by using the corresponding triplet-sensitized reactions. These alternatives to cyclization reactions initiated by visible light irradiation provide a new method for fabricating various functional devices with diarylethene derivatives.

A combined steady-state and time-resolved study of the excited-state dynamics of violacein in methanol, and several other solvent environments, was presented for the first time. The fluorescence quantum yields in the low-viscosity solvents methanol and acetone are on the order of 1 × 10-4, on par with the ultralow fluorescence quantum yields of the DNA/RNA nucleobases. Excited state decay occurs on a time scale of ~3 ps in methanol. Strikingly, the excited-state lifetime increases in more viscous solvents such as ethylene glycol and glycerol, with concomitant increases in fluorescence quantum yield. We hypothesize that excited violacein decays nonradiatively via a conical intersection that is accessed by large amplitude motions. Further work is warranted to understand the in vivo photophysics of this pigment and the role it plays in providing photoprotection for bacteria.

Accounting for perturbation theory, phosphorescence gains intensity from spin-allowed S-S and T-T electronic transitions via the spin-orbit coupling mixing of the singlet excited states manifold (Sn) with the first triplet (T1) excited state and of the triplet excited states manifold (Tn) with the ground singlet (S0) electronic state. A proper account of spin-orbit coupling makes it possible to estimate the main parameters of phosphorescence, like the transition dipole moment, radiative lifetime, and rate constant for each of the spin sublevels of the triplet state. The best equipment for the theoretical study of phosphorescence of today is, in our opinion, the quadratic-response theory formalism implemented in the DALTON program package, where this method is accessible at the HF, MCSCF, or DFT levels and where the spin-orbit operator can be accounted for exactly or by various effective approximations. The quadratic-response theory rests on an implicit sum-overstate principle, which allows one to describe correctly and largely clarify the phosphorescence mechanism for a number of difficult cases such as dioxygen (magnetic phosphorescence), benzene (vibronically induced phosphorescence), porphyrins (external and internal heavy atom effects), and cyclometalated iridium complexes (spin-sublevel selectivity and tuning of transition dipole moment orientation).

The temperature- and pressure-dependent kinetics and product yields from the C2H3 + C2H2 reaction were studied using time-resolved photoionization time-of-flight mass spectrometry (PI-TOF-MS) at 500 and 700 K and 5-50 Torr. Significant temperature- and pressure-dependent yields of C4H5, C4H4, and C6H6 were observed. The catalytic cycle leading to formation of C4H4 and C6H6 can be clearly observed under our experimental conditions (i.e.. much higher yields of products than the number of initial radicals), and the radical chain reactions responsible for these high product yields are elucidated by comparison with a pressure-dependent kinetic mechanism constructed from experimental and calculated reaction rates. Branching to the H-loss channel producing C4H4 increased with increasing temperature and decreasing pressure, while the yield of n-C4H5 from collisional stabilization increased with increasing pressure, indicating that C4H4 is formed primarily via the chemically activated pathway. The yield of C6H6 also increased at higher temperatures due to the increasing reaction rate of n-C4H5 + C2H2. To model the secondary chemistry leading to C6H6 formation at long time scales, several side reactions were added to the model to estimate the effect of wall reactions, reactions with the I atom, and radical-radical reactions. Additional experiments performed at high C2H2 concentrations produced large yields of C4H4 and C6H6, which were adequately predicted by the model without needing to account for side chemistry.

Although the reaction was discovered as its intermolecular variant, cyclization under NHTK conditions has been widely used in the recent years due to highly appealing factors from a synthetic point of view: (1) It is easy to obtain stable molecules with both aldehyde and haloalkene functionalities. (2) There is no need to use an excess of coupling partners. (3) A generally higher stereoselectivity is enjoyed than for intermolecular reactions. (4) There are higher yields than for its corresponding bimolecular analogue. (5) Polymerization products are absent. (6) The standard cyclization concentration ranges between 1 and 20 mM, facilitating the cyclization of linear precursors in relatively high concentration. This is an important factor to scale up synthetic processes. In comparison to other cyclization processes, NHTK affords this possibility without observing polymerization products.

dataset_item.question: How do different chemical environments influence the structural evolution and catalytic performance of nanomaterials composed of noble metals and 3d-transition metals?
dataset_item.answer:
Chemical environments play a critical role in the structural evolution and catalytic performance of nanomaterials composed of noble metals (NMs) and 3d-transition metals (3d-TMs). In electrocatalytic environments, electrolytes at the catalyst interface drive dynamic processes such as alloying, dealloying, and realloying, which create stable active sites with synergistic effects arising from lattice strain and electronic interactions between NMs and 3d-TMs. These processes enhance activity and durability while optimizing the use of NMs. Conversely, in gas-phase oxidative environments, surface oxygenation of 3d-TMs leads to the formation of core-shell structures with oxygenated 3d-TM shells and NM-rich cores. This structural evolution facilitates specific catalytic mechanisms, such as oxygen activation and reactant adsorption, which are critical for reactions like hydrocarbon oxidation.

These environment-dependent transformations—driven by electrochemical dissolution in liquid phases and surface oxidation in gas phases—create dynamic active sites that improve catalytic efficiency, stability, and reduce NM content. Advanced in situ techniques provide crucial insights into these processes, enabling the rational design of nanomaterials with tailored structures for energy and environmental applications.

### Task 1: Summary of Purpose  
The paper investigates the dynamic structural evolution of multimetallic nanomaterials containing noble metals (NMs) and 3d-transition metals (3d-TMs) under catalytic reaction conditions. It emphasizes understanding how core-shell and alloy arrangements of atoms change dynamically during reactions, as this structural evolution significantly impacts catalytic performance. The study highlights advanced techniques, particularly **in situ/operando synchrotron high-energy X-ray diffraction** and **pair distribution function analyses**, as key tools for characterizing these dynamic changes. The ultimate goal is to provide insights that inform the design of nanostructured catalysts for energy and environmental sustainability applications.

---

### Task 2: Classification of Purpose  
The paper emphasizes **"<method>"** because it focuses on employing advanced characterization techniques (e.g., synchrotron X-ray diffraction) to study the dynamic structural evolution of nanomaterials. While the results of these investigations are important, the central theme revolves around the methodologies used to gain insights into the atomic-scale structural dynamics.

---

### Task 3: Relevant Research Questions  
1. **Atomic-Scale Dynamics**: How do the core-shell and alloy structures of multimetallic nanomaterials evolve under various reaction conditions, such as temperature, adsorbates, and electrochemical potentials?  
2. **Catalytic Performance Correlation**: What is the relationship between the dynamic structural evolution of multimetallic nanomaterials and their catalytic performance?  
3. **Characterization Techniques**: How can in situ/operando synchrotron techniques and pair distribution function analyses be optimized for studying dynamic changes in NM/3d-TM nanostructures?  
4. **Material Design**: What structural or compositional features of NM/3d-TM nanomaterials enhance their stability and catalytic efficiency under dynamic operating conditions?  
5. **Reaction-Specific Evolution**: How do different chemical environments (e.g., fuel cell operating conditions, electrocatalytic reactions) uniquely influence the structural evolution of NM/3d-TM nanomaterials?  
6. **Sustainability Applications**: How can insights into structural dynamics be leveraged to design multimetallic nanocatalysts for applications in energy and environmental sustainability?  
7. **Formation Mechanisms**: What are the fundamental mechanisms driving core-shell and alloy structure formation, such as seed-mediated growth, thermochemical calcination, and chemical dealloying?  
8. **Material-Specific Behavior**: How do Pt- and Pd-based nanoparticles or nanowires alloyed with various 3d-TMs differ in their dynamic structural evolution and catalytic behavior?

inference_contexts: An overview of the explorations of multimetallic nanomaterials as electrocatalysts has indeed demonstrated a critical role of core-shell/alloy structural evolution under the reaction conditions in the activity and durability. Very often, such evolution could occur under both the post-synthesis processing and the reaction condition evolutions, e.g.. chemical/electrochemical dealloying and adsorbate-induced structural evolution, characteristic of the dynamic nature. While the dynamic process is complex, the ability to gain an insight into the evolution of core-shell and alloy structures is a significant advance. The understanding of the dynamic nature of 3d-TMs in core-shell/alloy evolution in acidic electrolytes remains elusive. The participation of 3d-TMs would greatly enhance the catalytic activity for chemical/electrochemical reactions by introducing lattice strain and ligand/electronic effect. While the perception of "Pt-skin" where 3d-TMs are completely buried under noble metal shells is well supported by high-resolution TEM data of individual NPs, there is increasing evidence for the synergistic participation of 3d-TMs on the catalyst as active sites in the form of a stable alloy structure for the electrochemical reactions. Such active and stable active sites are believed to be originated from the dynamic structure evolution of alloying-dealloying-realloying processes under the operating conditions. Understanding the exact structures of such active sites is important for developing new strategies to control activity and stability while reducing the noble metal content in the catalysts.

One important aspect for the structural evolution for NP/NW catalysts in general is the strong dependence on the chemical environment of the catalysts. In contrast to the above electrocatalysis examples where structural evolution could occur due to the presence of electrolyte at the catalyst interface which facilitates the dissolution of metal ions upon dealloying, the study of the same or similar nanocatalysts under gas-phase reaction conditions offers a different perspective to look at the core-shell structural evolution under reaction conditions. Understanding the dynamic processes of the core-shell/alloy structures under oxidative environments is not only for enhancing the catalytic performance in the gas-phase reaction, but also provides insight for the design of active and stable catalysts. For example, gas-phase hydrocarbon oxidation reactions have traditionally relied on oxygen-activation sites on the peripheral zones of oxide-supported noble metal catalysts. Recently, the initial alloying of NMs and 3d-TMs serves as an intriguing pathway for the design of active surface sites where the NMs provide adsorption site for CO and the surface-oxygenated 3d-TMs offer oxygen-activation sites. The NM/3d-TM alloy NPs undergo surface oxygenation, forming a CHA-type core with 3d-TM-oxygenated shell structure. Further understanding of the role of this type of structural evolution in enhancing activity and durability may lead to a new research frontier for the design of new-generation oxidation catalysts by tuning compositions and morphologies at the atomic scale. ,,, By highlighting the selected examples in connection with the recent advances in the field, this Account serves as a springboard from fundamental understanding of the core-shell and alloy structural dynamics to the broad applications of the nanostructured catalysts and electrocatalysts. There are still many challenging questions remaining to be answered, including how the atomic-scale arrangements of the surface active sites correlate with the nanophase structures of the NPs/NWs during the nanoscale dynamic processes, and how the structural durability of the catalysts in the catalytic processes can be controlled to enable the performance durability of the catalysts. Part of the ongoing investigations involves an in-depth understanding of factors controlling the composition optimization and the realloying under electrochemical and fuel cell operating conditions. Future studies will need to be advanced in several fronts, including the use of surface-sensitive techniques, especially under in situ/operando measurement modes, to probe the surface sites and surface/subsurface species, the design of multicomponent catalysts with nanoscale thermodynamic stability in the reactive environment, and the computational modeling of the atomic mobilities on and in the NPs/NWs in the presence of surface and interfacial species. These advancements will also benefit many areas of the applications of the NP and NW catalysts, especially in the area of energy and environmental sustainability.

With its elegant hourglass shape, the transmembrane helical bundle of the NOX/STEAP family of oxidoreductases can serve many functions. Its outer heme can direct electrons to diverse acceptors, such as molecular oxygen, ferric iron, and quinones. A distinct feature of this reaction is that it does not involve any covalent adduct with the heme iron, differently from the reactions catalyzed by heme proteins such as cytochrome P450s or the globins. As opposed to the close conservation of the transmembrane heme-binding scaffold, the cytosolic elements of these proteins are structurally diverse and unrelated. Their varying topologies feature characteristic quaternary structures, cofactor-binding sites and specificities, and regulatory elements. Despite the tremendous progress in the field, key questions remain open about the functioning of these enzymes. What are the structural mechanisms for the regulation of their enzymatic activities? How did their isoform-specific properties evolve? How do they prevent the escape of electrons to the membrane milieu that could cause membrane-damaging lipid oxidation? Will powerful and selective drugs be identified? Behind their seemingly simple catalyzed reactions, these enzymes strike for the intricacy of their biology and the complexity of their functional mechanisms that are made possible by the distinct elements that decorate their conserved heme-binding scaffold.

The core-shell/alloy structural dynamics of these nanomaterials are affected by the chemical environment, leading to changes in their catalytic activity and stability.

**Influence of Chemical Environment on Structural Evolution**

1.  **Electrochemical Environment**: In electrochemical reactions, the presence of electrolytes at the catalyst interface can facilitate the dissolution of metal ions, leading to dealloying and realloying processes. This dynamic process affects the core-shell structural evolution, with 3d-TMs participating as active sites in the form of stable alloy structures.

**Influence of Chemical Environment on Catalytic Performance**

1.  **Noble Metal Content**: The presence of 3d-TMs in core-shell/alloy structures enhances catalytic activity by introducing lattice strain and ligand/electronic effects. This can lead to improved catalytic performance and reduced noble metal content in the catalysts.
2.  **Surface Active Sites**: The dynamic structure evolution of alloying-dealloying-realloying processes under operating conditions creates active and stable surface sites. Understanding the exact structures of these active sites is crucial for developing new strategies to control activity and stability.

**Impact of Chemical Environment on Catalyst Durability**

1.  **Atomic-Scale Arrangements**: The correlation between atomic-scale arrangements of surface active sites and nanophase structures during dynamic processes is still not well understood.
2.  **Structural Durability**: The control of structural durability in catalytic processes is essential for maintaining catalyst performance. Investigating the factors controlling composition optimization and realloying under electrochemical and fuel cell operating conditions is essential.

**Future Directions**

1.  **Surface-Sensitive Techniques**: The use of surface-sensitive techniques, especially in situ/operando measurement modes, will be crucial for probing surface sites and surface/subsurface species.
2.  **Multicomponent Catalysts**: Designing multicomponent catalysts with nanoscale thermodynamic stability in reactive environments will be essential for achieving high-performance catalysts.
3.  **Computational Modeling**: Computational modeling of atomic mobilities on and in NPs/NWs in the presence of surface and interfacial species will provide valuable insights into the dynamic processes.

In conclusion, the chemical environment plays a critical role in the structural evolution and catalytic performance of nanomaterials composed of noble metals and 3d-TMs. Understanding the dynamic processes of core-shell/alloy structures under different chemical environments will enable the development of more efficient and durable catalysts for various applications.

dataset_item.question: How does phase-changing behavior in sulfolane and secondary amine solutions influence CO2 absorption rates and energy consumption during postcombustion CO2 capture?
dataset_item.answer: The phase-changing behavior of sulfolane and secondary amine solutions, specifically the sulfolane/2-methylaminoethanol (MAE) biphasic system at an optimal 4M/5M ratio, significantly enhances CO₂ absorption rates and improves energy efficiency during postcombustion CO₂ capture. This behavior enables higher CO₂ loading capacity while leveraging the inherent instability of carbamate C-N bonds in secondary amines, which facilitates faster desorption and reduces stripping energy consumption to 40.2% of that required by traditional 5M monoethanolamine (MEA) solutions. However, higher operating temperatures negatively impact absorption rates and energy savings. While this system demonstrates superior absorption kinetics and energy efficiency, further quantitative analysis of long-term energy consumption, environmental safety, and practical scalability is necessary to ensure its viability for industrial deployment.

dataset_item.question: How does the grain boundary structure affect ionic diffusion in cubic Na3PS4?
dataset_item.answer: The grain boundary (GB) structure in cubic Na₃PS₄ plays a critical role in determining ionic diffusion by influencing sodium vacancy segregation and trapping. Molecular dynamics and density functional theory (DFT) calculations show that GBs with higher vacancy segregation energies and fewer trapping sites reduce vacancy trapping, thereby enhancing ionic diffusivity. Factors such as GB orientation, symmetric tilt angles, and vacancy concentration directly affect ionic conduction. Engineering the GB structure through strategies like optimizing tilt angles or doping can mitigate vacancy blocking effects, improve ionic transport, and enhance the overall conductivity of polycrystalline Na₃PS₄ solid-state electrolytes.
dataset_item.topic:
### 1. Summary of the Paper's Purpose:
The purpose of the paper is to investigate the physical origin of reduced ionic conduction at grain boundaries (GBs) in polycrystalline solid-state electrolytes (SSEs). Through molecular dynamics simulations and first-principles calculations, the study identifies the role of GBs in ionic conduction, focusing on the thermodynamic-kinetic interaction between GBs and sodium (Na) vacancies in cubic Na₃PS₄. The findings highlight that reduced ionic conduction is due to the segregation of Na vacancies at the GB core, which depends on the GB structure, vacancy segregation energy, and the number of segregation sites. This work aims to guide the design of polycrystalline SSEs with improved ionic conductivity through grain boundary engineering.

### 2. Classification of Purpose:
The purpose of the paper emphasizes **"<result>"**, as the study provides specific insights into the mechanisms behind GB-induced ionic conduction retardation and suggests strategies for improving SSE performance.

### 3. Relevant Research Questions:
- What is the fundamental mechanism by which grain boundaries reduce ionic conduction in polycrystalline SSEs?
- How do the thermodynamic and kinetic interactions between grain boundaries and vacancies influence ionic transport in SSEs?
- What role does the structure of the grain boundary play in vacancy segregation and its effect on ionic conductivity?
- How can grain boundary engineering be utilized to enhance ionic conduction in polycrystalline SSEs?
- Are there specific grain boundary structures in cubic Na₃PS₄ that minimize vacancy segregation and maximize ionic conductivity?
- Can the insights from this study be generalized to other polycrystalline SSE materials beyond Na₃PS₄?

inference_contexts: DFT MD simulations indicate that higher Na-ion conductivity in Na3PS4 can be obtained by introducing Na-ion vacancies. Just 2% vacancies result in an order of magnitude larger conductivity (compared to the stoichiometric compound), reaching 0.20 S/cm, and a reduction in the activation energy from 0.28 to 0.16 eV. MD simulations of halogen-doped cubic Na3PS4 suggest a practical route toward charge compensated vacancies to raise the conductivity of this material. A systematic variation of the halogen dopants indicates that all halogens can increase the conductivity by raising the Na-vacancy concentration, with Br-doping leading to the best results. Not only vacancies appear vital for microscopic diffusion; the MD simulations indicate that free volume also plays a role in the transition mechanism. A large free volume induced by phonons enhances the chance for Na-ions to make a successful transition toward a neighboring site. The MD simulations also show that Na-conductivity in the cubic and tetragonal phase are similar; thus both phases of Na3PS4 are predicted to be highly conductive solid electrolytes. Furthermore, the orders of magnitude difference between the MD simulations and experiments suggest that macroscopic conductivity can be significantly increased by reducing the grain boundary resistance, which is most likely one of the major bottlenecks toward high performance solid state batteries. The Na2 (12d)-site in the cubic phase, connecting the occupied Na1 (6b)-sites, has been shown to be metastable, and upon increased Na-ion conductivity the time averaged Na2-site occupancy increases with increasing vacancy concentrations and/or higher temperatures due to an increase in Na1 → Na1 transitions. Thereby present DFT MD simulations reveal the diffusion mechanism and potential routes toward larger Na-ion conductivities in Na3PS4.

In summary, we revealed the origin for distinct activation energies of Na-ion conduction in Na3SbS4 during the phase transition from the tetragonal to cubic structure through the combination of real-time impedance analysis, DFT simulations, and in situ quasi-elastic neutron scattering. From the experimental Arrhenius plot, the activation energy dramatically decreased from 0.224 eV for t-Na3SbS4 to 0.036 eV for c-Na3SbS4. This trend was explained by DFT calculations from comparison of the energy barrier per moving Na atom in the tetragonal phase (0.45 eV) with that in cubic Na3SbS4 (0.12 eV). Furthermore, the neutron scattering results showed that such distinct values of activation energies are associated with the Na-ion jump during the diffusion process in tetragonal and cubic crystalline structures. Cubic Na3SbS4 exhibited a shorter jump length (2.85 Å) and larger diffusion coefficient (2.07 × 10-10 m2 S-1) than the tetragonal structure (4.83 Å and 1.25 × 10-10 m2 S-1). This research provides insights into Na-ion diffusion in solid electrolytes with different crystalline structures. These results provide guidance for the design of novel Na-ion conductors and contribute to the development of all-solid-state Na batteries.

In this study, molecular dynamic simulations and the DFT energy calculations are performed to analyze the effect of GB orientation and vacancy concentration on the ionic diffusion in cubic Na3PS4. The blocking effects in the GB core strongly depend on the vacancy distribution in the GB structure, which is determined by both the segregation energy and the number of trapping sites available in the GB core. It can be deduced that the GB interfaces with higher segregation energy and fewer trapping sites in the GB core are expected to achieve a higher ionic diffusivity in polycrystalline solid-state electrolytes. The strategies of improving the ionic transport of polycrystalline solid electrolyte can concentrate on GB engineering, for instance, by tuning symmetric tilting angle of GB and doping to adjust the energy variation in GB core.

In order to get insight into the gas-sensing mechanisms of single-crystalline and polycrystalline nanostructures, in this work the single-crystalline (SC) NiO nanosheets and the polycrystalline (PC) NiO nanosheets are successfully synthesized through a simple solvothermal method. The morphology characteristic results show that the SC NiO consists of the mesoporous single-crystalline nanosheets, whereas the irregular polycrystalline nanosheets composed of nanoparticles are clearly observed in the PC NiO. The SC NiO exhibits the similar specific surface area and mesoporosity as the PC NiO. The as-prepared SC NiO performs a largely enhanced sensitivity to NO2 at room temperature compared to the PC NiO. According to the fitting results of EIS, the interface resistance exhibits the dominant effect both in the SC NiO and the PC NiO, compared to the ignorable contact resistance between the electrode and NiO. Furthermore, it is found that an extra grain boundary resistance exists in the PC NiO. Though the chemisorption of NO2 on NiO increases the hole concentration both in the SC NiO and the PC NiO, the surface-adsorbed NO2 molecules also introduce the surface states that can remarkably enhance the free carrier scattering at the grain boundary due to the electrostatic interaction between the chemisorbed NO2 molecules and the holes in NiO. Because the extra grain boundaries between the nanoparticles in the PC NiO nanosheets arouse the larger scattering potential inside the nanosheets after being exposed to NO2 gas, the carrier mobility decreases. However, due to the absence of grain boundary in the SC NiO nanosheets, the chemisorption of NO2 gives less influence on the carrier mobility so that the SC NiO performs the largely enhanced sensitivity. Here we hope that this work can help us to further understand the gas sensing mechanism and open up a new generation of gas sensors.
