inference_contexts: For biomedical applications, the use of in situ forming hydrogels is preferred over preformed hydrogels since there is no need for surgical interventions as gelation can take place under physiological conditions upon injection. Furthermore, the initial fluidic nature of the precursor solution ensures proper shape adaptation and biological components can be incorporated in the hydrogel by simple mixing with the precursor polymer solution. , Physical cross-links, such as hydrophobic or ionic interactions, can be formed in situ under mild conditions, but the resulting hydrogels generally degrade or dissolve rapidly. Injectable chemically cross-linked hydrogels have been frequently prepared by photocuring polymers functionalized with vinylic groups. Although the presence of photoinitiators and the generated radicals in the polymerization process has been associated with cytotoxicity, frequently good cell compatibility is found for cells encapsulated in this type of hydrogel. , However, important drawbacks of photo-cross-linkable systems include the limited penetration depth of UV radiation and its potentially damaging effects on living tissue. In situ forming hydrogels utilizing covalent cross-linking between polymers with complementary functional groups therefore received much attention in the last two decades. Early examples of chemical cross-linking reactions forming hydrogels include Schiff base formation between aldehydes and amines and the Passerini and Ugi condensation. However, remaining functional groups on polymers may react with functional groups present in biomolecules such as proteins, limiting the application of these hydrogels as in situ forming delivery systems. In this regard, the use of chemoselective, bioorthogonal cross-linking strategies, which do not interfere with biochemical processes or biomolecules, are very appealing. The most investigated chemoselective cross-linking reaction for hydrogels is the Cu (I)-catalyzed Huisgen 1,3-dipolar cycloaddition of terminal alkynes and azides, commonly known as click chemistry. This term was originally coined in 2001 by Sharpless et al. for a number of new regiospecific linking reactions that give high yields and generally require no purification. The first hydrogel cross-linked via click chemistry was described by the group of Hilborn and was based on PVA. Although this category of hydrogels has been mainly used for tissue engineering applications, they have also been applied for the controlled release of therapeutics and different biomolecules, including doxorubicin bovine serum albumin (BSA) and pDNA. Because "classical" alkyne-azide cycloadditions require the use of a copper catalyst, which may cause adverse effects in biomedical applications, the use of strain-promoted azide-alkyne cycloaddition (SPAAC) is attracting increasing interest. This reaction employs the inherent ring strain of cyclooctyne groups to achieve fast and efficient cross-linking without the need for catalysts or external stimuli such as UV light. Hermann et al. reported on PEG hydrogels for the delivery of bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) inhibitors to treat excessive postoperative bone regrowth (resynostosis) after surgical correction of premature fusion of cranial sutures (craniosynostosis) in children. Mixing poly [(tetraethylene glycol methacrylate)-co-(azidotetraethylene glycol methacrylate)] with a 4-dibenzocyclooctynol PEG cross-linker resulted in the formation of hydrogels within 30 s, as demonstrated by oscillatory rheology. In vitro release experiments showed that the BMP inhibitor Gremlin1 remained bioactive when it was incorporated in the hydrogels by dissolution in the prepolymer solutions, confirming the bioorthogonal character of the SPAAC cross-linking method. When the prepolymer solutions were injected together with Gremlin1 in a surgically created cranial defect in weanling mice, a hydrogel formed in situ that was able to provide a controlled release of the inhibitor for 14 days. Following this approach, the authors were able to delay, but not completely prevent, postoperative bone regrowth in the cranial defect model. Since the ultimate goal of resynostosis therapy is to slow the postoperative bone growth for a period, but then allow the bone to regrow as the child ages, the reported approach holds promise as treatment after surgical intervention in craniosynostosis. Other emerging bioorthogonal strategies for the preparation of chemically cross-linked hydrogels include thiol-ene/yne reactions, , oxime chemistry, native chemical ligation, , and Diels-Alder cycloadditions. , Table presents a summary of several click chemistry strategies that have been used to form hydrogels, including advantages and disadvantages of each method. Dove and co-workers recently reported on the simultaneous application of thiol-yne and Diels-Alder chemistry to independently create two interpenetrating networks in a one-step procedure (Figure ). A loose network was prepared from norbornene-functionalized chitosan and linear PEG-ditetrazine, while a dense network was constructed by cross-linking 4-arm PEG-tetraalkyne with linear PEG-dithiol. The resulting double network hydrogels displayed a high compressive stress of 15 MPa at 98% compression without fracture or hysteresis upon repeated load. The hydrogels were postfunctionalized with a thiol-containing fluorescent dye and tetrazine-modified biotin via reaction with unreacted alkyne and norbornene groups, respectively. The cross-linking reactions were suggested to be bioorthogonal because of the high viability of human mesenchymal stem cells, which were encapsulated by adding them to the prepolymer solutions prior to hydrogel formation. An extensive recent review concerning bioorthogonal chemistries for hydrogel cross-linking can be found in ref .

The above examples show that several bioorthogonal reactions have emerged as innovative and versatile strategies to construct new functional hydrogels due to their high coupling efficiency, chemoselectivity, and mild reaction conditions. Although many of the described cross-linking reactions are believed to be bioorthogonal, caution should still be used when hydrogels are cross-linked in the presence of biomolecules, most notably proteins. The group of Gopferich investigated the compatibility of a number of reactive groups present on polymers, including maleimide and thiol groups, with lysozyme. Hydrogel preparation was simulated by using polymer/lysozyme mixtures and the possible conjugation of polymer chains to lysozyme was determined by SDS-PAGE analysis. Upon incubation with PEG-maleimide or PEG-thiol several protein modifications were indeed detected, which may affect the protein structure, adversely affect its activity and increase the risk of unwanted immune responses. This study indicates that side reactions between biomolecules and polymers, and possible strategies to prevent these, should always be considered when developing new hydrogels for therapeutic delivery and that the stability of each released biomolecule must be carefully evaluated for all cross-linking conditions in question. For example, cross-linking can be performed in slightly acidic solutions below pH 5 in order to decrease the nucleophilicity of amino groups by protonation and reduce their reactivity in Michael-type addition reactions. To protect proteins during radical polymerizations, Censi et al. managed to retain protein activity during photopolymerization of methacrylate groups by separating hydrophobic polymerization sites from more hydrophilic protein-containing areas.

In this Account, we have summarized our recent work on the construction of various bioinspired systems by integrating bioorthogonal chemistry with cell-membrane-based biomimetic approaches. The site-specific introduction of bioorthogonal groups through cellular biosynthesis and metabolic incorporation is beneficial to retain the native structures and functions of cell membranes. Meanwhile, the exclusive and fast reaction capability of bioorthogonal ligations provides additional chemical or biological performances such as labeling, targeting, imaging, and therapy, enabling the biomimetic systems to serve versatile theranostic nanoplatforms. What is more, such a strategy can be applied in not only cell membranes but also cell vesicles or living cells, further broadening the choice scope and design flexibility of the biomimetic systems.

The minimalistic molecular design of polyphosphazenes in the present study affords biodegradability and surprisingly impressive multifunctionality while maintaining a reasonably direct pathway to further development and potential manufacturing. Temperature- and composition-dependent degradation profiles observed in this study can provide ample opportunities for modulating pharmacokinetics and solving shelf life challenges. Perhaps one of the most important features of polyphosphazene copolymers, although requiring further exploration, is their demonstrated ability to self-assemble in aqueous solutions upon variation in environmental conditions. Although nanogel formation upon cross-linking with multivalent spermine was not completely unexpected, the pH-induced aggregation leading to narrow polydispersity nanoassemblies can introduce new dimensions in nanoscale engineering of delivery vehicles with required hydrophobicity, size, hydration sphere, and electrostatic potential. Synthesized biodegradable polyphosphazenes have already demonstrated their potential for intracellular delivery by facilitating cell-surface interactions and uptake of cargo protein by cancer cells.

In summary, we have demonstrated an entirely protein-based hydrogel with multienergy dissipation modes and tunable dynamic response using the heterodimeric coiled coil CCE/CCK as a physical cross-linking mechanism. Due to the temperature dependent association/dissociation of the CCE/CCK complexes and the network structures of the protein network, the hydrogels exhibit broad and dual dissipation modes, and the dynamic properties of the hydrogels can be further tuned by the protein concentrations and the stoichiometric ratios of two components (CCE- and CCK-containing elastomeric proteins). Moreover, the fast association/dissociation kinetics of the CCE/CCK complexes endowed the protein hydrogel with excellent shear-thinning and rapid self-healing abilities, making this protein hydrogel a unique injectable hydrogel system. These unique properties may open up avenues toward a range of biomedical applications for this protein hydrogel. Moreover, we anticipate that the interplay between the cross-linker dynamics and the hydrogel network structures may offer a new perspective for the design of injectable dynamic hydrogels in the future.

The advantages of bioorthogonal cross-linking strategies for hydrogel formation in therapeutic delivery applications are:

1.  **Chemoselectivity**: Bioorthogonal cross-linking reactions do not interfere with biochemical processes or biomolecules, ensuring that the cross-linking process does not damage or alter the therapeutic molecules being delivered.
2.  **Mild reaction conditions**: Bioorthogonal reactions often occur under mild conditions, making them suitable for use in biological systems.
3.  **High coupling efficiency**: Bioorthogonal reactions tend to have high coupling efficiency, allowing for the formation of stable and effective hydrogels.
4.  **Flexibility**: Bioorthogonal reactions can be designed to occur under various conditions, such as different temperatures, pH levels, or solvent conditions, making them versatile for various applications.
5.  **Low toxicity**: Bioorthogonal reactions are designed to be non-toxic and biocompatible, reducing the risk of adverse reactions or toxicity.

The limitations of bioorthogonal cross-linking strategies for hydrogel formation in therapeutic delivery applications are:

1.  **Potential for side reactions**: Even bioorthogonal reactions can sometimes lead to side reactions with biomolecules, which can affect the stability or activity of the therapeutic molecules being delivered.
2.  **Dependence on reaction conditions**: Bioorthogonal reactions can be sensitive to reaction conditions, such as temperature, pH, or solvent, which can affect the efficiency and selectivity of the reaction.
3.  **Limited accessibility**: Some bioorthogonal reactions may require specialized equipment or expertise to perform, limiting their accessibility for researchers without extensive experience.
4.  **Cost**: Some bioorthogonal reagents can be expensive, making them less accessible for large-scale applications.
5.  **Limited understanding of mechanisms**: The mechanisms of bioorthogonal reactions are not always fully understood, which can make it challenging to optimize or predict the outcome of the reaction.

Examples of bioorthogonal cross-linking strategies include:

1.  **Click chemistry**: The Cu(I)-catalyzed Huisgen 1,3-dipolar cycloaddition of terminal alkynes and azides is a widely used bioorthogonal reaction for hydrogel formation.
2.  **Strain-promoted azide-alkyne cycloaddition (SPAAC)**: This reaction uses the inherent ring strain of cyclooctyne groups to achieve fast and efficient cross-linking without the need for catalysts or external stimuli.
3.  **Thiol-ene/yne reactions**: These reactions involve the addition of thiols to alkenes or alkynes, which can be used for hydrogel formation.
4.  **Oxime chemistry**: Oxime reactions involve the formation of oximes from aldehydes and amines, which can be used for hydrogel formation.
5.  **Diels-Alder cycloadditions**: These reactions involve the addition of dienes to dienophiles, which can be used for hydrogel formation.

In summary, bioorthogonal cross-linking strategies offer several advantages for hydrogel formation in therapeutic delivery applications, including chemoselectivity, mild reaction conditions, high coupling efficiency, flexibility, and low toxicity. However, they also have limitations, such as potential side reactions, dependence on reaction conditions, limited accessibility, cost, and limited understanding of mechanisms.

dataset_item.question: How is the apparent activation energy calculated using Friedman's isoconversional method for polymer degradation?
dataset_item.answer: Friedman's isoconversional method is used to calculate the apparent activation energy (Eₐ) for polymer degradation by analyzing the relationship between the conversion rate and temperature. At a fixed degree of conversion (e.g., 5%), the natural logarithm of the conversion rate (ln(dα/dt)) is plotted against the inverse of temperature (1/T). The slope of the resulting straight line is equal to -Eₐ/R, where R is the universal gas constant. By performing this analysis at different heating rates (β) and for multiple conversion intervals, the method provides a model-free determination of Eₐ without assuming a specific reaction mechanism, making it highly versatile for complex degradation processes.

The purpose of this paper is to investigate the thermal degradation kinetics of polypropylene (PP) and a polypropylene/starch blend (PP/S, 70/30 wt %) after exposure to natural weathering for four years, as compared to unexposed samples stored under laboratory conditions. The study employs nonisothermal thermogravimetry at varying heating rates to determine kinetic parameters using multiple model-free and model-fitting analytical methods. Additionally, a mathematical model was developed to describe the degradation mechanism and estimate kinetic parameters for the PP/S blend. The research examines how natural weathering and starch addition influence the degradation mechanism, thermal stability, and kinetic parameters of the materials.

---

Friedman's isoconversional method for calculating the apparent activation energy of polymer degradation involves the following steps:

1. Perform non-isothermal degradation experiments at different heating rates (β).
2. Calculate the conversion of the reaction (α) at each heating rate.
3. Plot ln(dα/dt) vs 1/T at a fixed value of α (e.g., 5%).
4. The resulting plot should be a straight line with a slope equal to E_a/R, where E_a is the apparent activation energy and R is the gas constant.
5. Repeat steps 2-4 for different intervals of α to obtain multiple values of E_a/R.
6. Plot the values of E_a/R obtained at different α intervals against the corresponding α values.
7. The apparent activation energy (E_a) can be calculated from the slope of the plot in step 6, using the equation: E_a = R \* slope.

Note that this method assumes that the reaction mechanism remains the same at all α intervals, and that the reaction rate is only dependent on temperature. The apparent activation energy calculated using this method is a function of the reaction conversion (α).

Alternatively, you can also use the Friedman's equation to calculate the apparent activation energy directly from the non-isothermal degradation data:

ln(dα/dt) = ln(A_0 \* f(α)) - E_a/R \* 1/T

where dα/dt is the reaction rate, A_0 is the pre-exponential factor, f(α) is the reaction model, E_a is the apparent activation energy, and R is the gas constant.

By rearranging this equation, you can obtain:

E_a = R \* (-ln(dα/dt) - ln(A_0 \* f(α))) / (1/T)

This equation can be used to calculate the apparent activation energy at each α interval, and the resulting values can be plotted against α to obtain the apparent activation energy as a function of reaction conversion.

dataset_item.question: How does grafting PNIPAm onto an MC backbone and concurrent cross-linking contribute to thermal hysteresis behavior in PNIPAm-g-MC hydrogel?
dataset_item.answer:
Grafting PNIPAm onto a methylcellulose (MC) backbone and concurrently cross-linking it creates a hydrogel with a thermal hysteresis of 10°C during its volume phase transition. This thermal hysteresis arises from the formation of stable hydrophobic junctions within the MC scaffold, which enhance the difference between the hydrogel's shrinking behavior during heating and its expansion during cooling. These junctions provide structural stability and enable programmable thermal responses.  

When combined with photothermal magnetite nanoparticles (MNPs), the PNIPAm-g-MC hydrogel exhibits light-triggered shrinking and cooling-induced recovery, enabling programmable volume changes and the ability to memorize irradiation history. This unique behavior is demonstrated in applications such as bilayer actuators, which show static bending under light exposure, and in devices inspired by origami, microvalves, and drug delivery systems. The combination of thermal hysteresis and light-responsive properties makes the hydrogel suitable for advanced programmable material applications.

This combination leads to a large thermal hysteresis of 10 °C in the volume phase transition of the hydrogel.

dataset_item.question: What are the limitations and accuracy challenges associated with thermal imaging in heterogeneous catalytic reactions under microwave heating?
dataset_item.answer:
Thermal imaging in microwave-heated heterogeneous catalytic reactions provides valuable real-time, two-dimensional temperature mapping, with the capability to monitor temperatures up to 1000 °C. However, its accuracy faces significant challenges due to the multiparameter dependence of emissivity. Factors such as the gaseous reaction environment, varying media, object-to-camera distance, microwave field distribution, and the non-uniform emissivity of the catalyst bed can lead to inaccurate temperature measurements. 

These limitations are exacerbated in microwave-heated reactors, where nonhomogeneous heating profiles and localized hot spots are common. Consequently, relying solely on thermal imaging is insufficient for precise temperature monitoring. A dual measurement approach that integrates thermal imaging with at least one contact sensor (e.g., a thermocouple) is essential. This combined methodology enhances reliability by mitigating risks and ensuring accurate temperature readings, as demonstrated in methane dry reforming over a platinum-on-carbon catalyst.

dataset_item.question: How does the second osmotic virial coefficient vary with temperature and solvent composition in ternary polymer solutions?
dataset_item.answer:
The second osmotic virial coefficient (\( B_2 \)) in ternary polymer solutions exhibits a complex dependence on temperature and solvent composition due to competitive solvation effects and the interplay between miscibility transitions. For a fixed solvent composition, \( B_2 \) vanishes at multiple Θ temperatures (\( T_{\Theta} \)), transitioning between positive (miscible) and negative (immiscible) values. Between two distinct Θ temperatures (\( T_{\Theta}^{(1)} \) and \( T_{\Theta}^{(2)} \)), \( B_2 \) becomes negative, indicating phase separation, while outside this range, it becomes positive, signaling miscibility. This behavior reflects the presence of a closed-loop immiscibility region in the phase diagram.  

Adjusting the solvent composition introduces additional complexity. For an initial solvent composition \( r_o = 5 \), the system exhibits two Θ temperatures. However, reducing the solvent ratio to \( r_o = 0.942 \) results in three Θ temperatures, reflecting combined upper critical solution temperature (UCST) and closed-loop phase behavior. This shift highlights how solvent composition influences miscibility transitions, with \( \Delta T_{\Theta} = T_{\Theta}^{(2)} - T_{\Theta}^{(1)} \) serving as a universal measure of immiscibility. As \( r_o \) decreases, miscibility improves, shrinking the range of immiscibility and reducing the upper critical solution temperature, while the lower critical solution temperature remains nearly constant.  

Overall, \( B_2 \) serves as a direct indicator of phase stability: positive values correspond to miscibility, while negative values signal phase separation. Its variation with temperature and solvent composition reveals the rich and intricate phase behavior of ternary polymer solutions, including the emergence of multiple miscibility transitions and changes in the phase diagram structure.

The second osmotic virial coefficient B 2 for the UCST binary polymer solution C/B, whose phase diagram is denoted by the blue curve in Figure , vanishes only at a single Θ temperature T Θ. (The temperature variation of B 2 ( T ) for the C/B mixture is omitted from Figure to avoid overlapping of the Θ points of the C/B and A/B/C solutions.)

Complementary information about general trends in miscibility of ternary A/B/C polymer solutions that emerge from Figures and can be deduced by considering the second osmotic virial coefficient B 2 ( T = const . ) as a function of the composition of the pure solvent mixture maintained in osmotic equilibrium with the polymer solution. Figure provides examples of plots of B 2 ( T = const . ) versus r oo for two temperatures coinciding with the Θ temperatures T Θ (1) and T Θ (2) deduced from Figure . The green and red curves, B 2 ( ϕ A oo , T = T Θ ( 2 ) ) and B 2 ( ϕ A oo , T = T Θ ( 1 ) ) of Figure intersect each other at a common point with the abcissa B 2 = 0 and the ordinate r oo = 5. Surprisingly, the second virial coefficient B 2 ( ϕ A oo , T = T Θ ( 1 ) ) also vanishes for r oo = 0.942. Figure resolves the seeming inconsistency in the presence of multiple Θ points by depicting the temperature variation of B 2 for a ternary A/B/C polymer solution with r o = 0.942. More specifically, Figure manifests the presence of three separate Θ temperatures T Θ (1), T Θ (2), and T Θ (3) for this particular system. Interestingly, the Θ temperature T Θ (2) of Figure coincides with the lower Θ temperature T Θ (1) = 279 K for the ternary polymer solution with r o = 5 in Figure . Figure also suggests that the ternary polymer solution (r o = 0.942) should be miscible at temperatures T for which B 2 ( T ) becomes positive, i.e, ranging from T Θ (1) to T Θ (2) or exceeding T Θ (3). The existence of these three separate Θ temperatures becomes more understandable by reference to the system's phase boundary depicted in Figure . The phase diagram of this particular system combines a UCST branch at low temperatures and a closed-loop region of immiscibility at higher temperatures, thereby directly predicting the appearance of three characteristic temperatures for phase separation, and thus of three separate Θ temperatures. Notice that Figures and are perfectly consistent and reflect the well-known thermodynamic regularity that miscibility and imiscibility occur, respectively, at temperatures for which B 2 is positive and negative. Measurements of B 2 , thus, can provide crucial information about miscibility when direct experimental determination of the phase diagrams may be very tedious as is in the case of ternary mixtures. dataset_item.question: How can genetically encoded photo-cross-linkers be optimized to simultaneously capture promiscuous binding partners and identify interaction interfaces?
dataset_item.answer: Genetically encoded photo-cross-linkers can be optimized by incorporating multifunctional features, such as selenium-based cleavable linkers, which enable simultaneous capture of transient protein interactions and identification of interaction interfaces. These enhancements improve compatibility with advanced proteomic strategies like CAPP-DIGE and IMAPP, facilitating the profiling of native chaperone clients and mapping their binding interfaces under dynamic or stress conditions. This approach is particularly valuable for studying intrinsically disordered and conditionally disordered proteins, which often exhibit promiscuous and transient binding behavior. While challenges remain, such as capturing ultrafast interactions or determining binding affinities, the versatility of selenium-based cleavable linkers and the potential for further functionalization with novel chemical groups promise broader applicability across diverse research areas. Additionally, integrating biocompatible and chemically cleavable tools could extend their utility to other fields requiring precise interaction mapping and transient protein analysis.

dataset_item.question: How can phasor-based analysis quantify contributions of multiple fluorescent components in imaging data?
dataset_item.answer: Phasor-based analysis quantifies contributions of multiple fluorescent components in imaging data by leveraging the geometric properties of phasor plots and the phasor rule of addition. Prior knowledge of the individual components' phasor positions is required, ensuring that these positions are not collinear. Multicomponent analysis becomes feasible if the phasor positions form a polygon, with each fluorescent species at the vertices, and the overall phasor cloud lies within this polygon. The quantitative contributions of each component are determined by projecting the phasor cloud onto axes defined by the polygon geometry. This approach is particularly effective for analyzing up to three components from single-frequency FLIM data, simplifying the separation of overlapping signals such as free NADH, enzyme-bound NADH, and lipid droplets. Unlike non-Euclidean methods, this technique provides a more intuitive and computationally efficient framework for multicomponent fluorescence analysis.

Phasor-based analysis is a method used in fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy (FLIM) to quantify contributions of multiple fluorescent components in imaging data. This approach is based on the concept of phasors, which are complex numbers that represent the amplitude and phase of a sinusoidal signal.

In the context of FLIM, the phasor approach involves representing the fluorescence lifetime distribution of a sample as a phasor cloud in a complex plane. Each point in the phasor cloud corresponds to a specific fluorescence lifetime value, with the real part representing the phase and the imaginary part representing the modulation frequency.

In the context of control valves, the preprocessing and postprocessing steps are crucial for reliable stiction detection. Stiction, a type of friction between surfaces, can occur in control valves and cause oscillations in the valve's movement. These oscillations can be detrimental to the valve's performance and overall system operation. To detect stiction accurately, data preprocessing and postprocessing are essential.

**Preprocessing Steps:**

1.  **Noise reduction:** Remove high-frequency noise from the data to prevent false positives and improve signal-to-noise ratio.
2.  **Data filtering:** Apply filters to remove unwanted frequency components or trend removal to focus on the signal of interest.
3.  **Data normalization:** Normalize the data to a common scale to prevent differences in amplitude from affecting the analysis.
4.  **Feature extraction:** Extract relevant features from the data, such as peak amplitudes, frequencies, or time-domain features, that are indicative of stiction.

**Postprocessing Steps:**

1.  **Peak identification:** Identify peaks in the data that correspond to stiction events.
2.  **Peak clustering:** Group similar peaks together to identify patterns or trends in the data.
3.  **Event detection:** Detect stiction events based on the identified peaks and patterns.
4.  **Classification:** Classify the detected events as either stiction or non-stiction based on predefined criteria.

**Example of Preprocessing and Postprocessing Methods:**

Some common preprocessing and postprocessing methods used in stiction detection include:

1.  **Wavelet denoising:** Removes high-frequency noise from the data using wavelet transforms.
2.  **Savitzky-Golay filtering:** Applies a low-pass filter to smooth the data and remove high-frequency components.
3.  **Moving average:** Averages neighboring data points to reduce noise and highlight trends.
4.  **Peak detection algorithms:** Identify peaks in the data using algorithms such as the Savitzky-Golay peak detection algorithm or the peak finder algorithm.
5.  **Machine learning algorithms:** Train machine learning models to classify stiction events based on extracted features.

In summary, preprocessing and postprocessing steps are essential for reliable stiction detection in control valves. By applying various techniques such as noise reduction, filtering, normalization, feature extraction, peak identification, peak clustering, event detection, and classification, engineers can improve the accuracy of stiction detection and prevent false positives or false negatives.

dataset_item.question: What are the differences in the electronic origin bands and low-frequency intermolecular modes between para-fluorophenol-cyclopropylamine and para-fluorophenol-ammonia complexes?
dataset_item.answer: The para-fluorophenol-cyclopropylamine (pFP-CPA) complex exhibits a significantly larger spectral red shift (816 cm⁻¹ for the endo conformer) in its S₁←S₀ electronic origin transition compared to the para-fluorophenol-ammonia (pFP-NH₃) complex. This larger red shift is attributed to cyclopropylamine's higher proton affinity and stronger hyperconjugative charge transfer interaction energy compared to ammonia. Additionally, the pFP-CPA complex displays significantly more intense low-frequency intermolecular vibrational modes in its fluorescence excitation spectrum, indicating a greater geometry change upon electronic excitation. This geometry change is further corroborated by the long progression observed in dispersed fluorescence spectra when the intermolecular stretching fundamental is excited. Computational spectral simulations using CAM-B3LYP/6-311++G(2d,2p) calculations and PGOPHER fitting confirm these findings, providing a detailed understanding of the electronic and vibrational differences between the two complexes.

dataset_item.question: How is the uncertainty of carbon emission results in wood utilization scenarios analyzed using probabilistic methods?
dataset_item.answer: The uncertainty of carbon emission results in wood utilization scenarios is analyzed using probabilistic methods, primarily Monte Carlo simulation. This approach involves running 10,000 deterministic computations, where input parameters are sampled from defined probability distributions to capture variability in key variables such as substitution credits and forest carbon sink impacts. The resulting outcomes are expressed as probability distributions and classified using IPCC terminology (e.g., "very likely" for 90-100% probability) to provide clear probabilistic interpretations. To further assess the influence of individual variables on overall uncertainty, sensitivity analysis is conducted using Spearman’s rank correlation (ρ), which quantifies the contribution of each input variable. This comprehensive methodology ensures robust uncertainty quantification and provides a clearer understanding of wood utilization’s climate mitigation potential over a 100-year horizon.

dataset_item.question: What are the crystal structures and stoichiometric compositions of TBPO semiclathrate hydrates in binary and double hydrate systems?
dataset_item.answer:
TBPO semiclathrate hydrates in binary (TBPO-H₂O) and double hydrate (TBPO-H₂O-CH₄) systems crystallize in the orthorhombic structure with the *Pbam* space group. The idealized unit cell composition is 4H·4P·4T·14D·148H₂O, corresponding to a structural stoichiometry of TBPO·34.5H₂O. Analytical measurements yield a stoichiometry of TBPO·(33.6 ± 0.9)H₂O, with deviations attributed to structural defects. 

In the double hydrate system, methane predominantly occupies the small D cages of the TBPO hydrate framework, with a maximum cage occupancy of approximately 85% at 8.5 MPa. The double hydrate retains the same orthorhombic structure and a similar H₂O:TBPO molar ratio as the binary hydrate. Methane storage capacity ranges between 61.6–74.6 mL/g in ~26–30 wt% TBPO solutions, demonstrating superior performance compared to THF and TBAB hydrates by at least 1.5×. Raman spectroscopy confirms selective methane occupancy in the D cages, with no evidence of structural alterations. These properties suggest potential applications in gas separation and thermal energy storage.

dataset_item.question: How does the temperature-responsive behavior of PNIPAAM grafted onto halloysite nanotubes influence properties such as colloidal stability and wettability?
dataset_item.answer: The temperature-responsive behavior of poly(N-isopropylacrylamide) (PNIPAAM) grafted onto halloysite nanotubes significantly impacts both colloidal stability and wettability due to its characteristic coil-to-globule transition at the lower critical solution temperature (LCST). Below the LCST, PNIPAAM remains in a hydrated, coiled state, enhancing colloidal stability through steric hindrance and promoting hydrophilic interactions that increase wettability. Above the LCST, PNIPAAM collapses into a globular state, reducing steric stabilization and making the surface more hydrophobic, which restricts water spreading. This thermoresponsive behavior modulates the Brownian diffusion and electrophoretic mobility of the hybrid nanocarriers, making these properties highly dependent on temperature. Furthermore, the wettability transition enables applications such as controlled drug delivery, where the hydrophilic state below LCST protects the drug, while the hydrophobic state above LCST facilitates its release. The combination of temperature-dependent colloidal stability, wettability, and transport properties makes PNIPAAM-grafted halloysite nanotubes highly suitable for stimuli-responsive applications.

dataset_item.question: What are the relative contributions of food processing, retail, wholesale, and human consumption to avoidable food waste in Norway?
dataset_item.answer: In Norway, human consumption is the largest contributor to avoidable food waste (AFW), generating 92 kt dry matter (DM) per year. This exceeds the combined AFW from food processing (33 kt DM/year), retail (29 kt DM/year), and wholesale (1 kt DM/year). Wholesale plays a negligible role in AFW generation, while food processing and retail contribute significantly. Losses from human consumption represent approximately 10% of total consumer-purchased food, underscoring the critical role of consumer behavior in AFW generation. Addressing waste at the consumption stage would yield the greatest impact in minimizing Norway's avoidable food waste, followed by interventions in food processing and retail.

dataset_item.question: How does planarity in the structure of flavonoid molecules influence their binding affinity toward G4 DNA?
dataset_item.answer:
Planarity in the structure of flavonoid molecules plays a crucial role in their binding affinity toward G4 DNA. Fisetin, a planar flavonoid with a coplanar conformation facilitated by the presence of a C2-C3 double bond in its C-ring, exhibits stronger binding to G4 DNA compared to naringenin, which lacks this double bond and adopts a noncoplanar conformation relative to the ring A/C plane. The planar structure of fisetin enables efficient π-π stacking interactions with the external bases of G4 DNA, while naringenin's noncoplanar conformation hinders such interactions, favoring binding to duplex DNA instead. Furthermore, fisetin forms a greater number of hydrogen bonds with G4 DNA, enhancing its binding affinity.

Spectroscopic and molecular docking studies confirm that fisetin's planar structure facilitates interaction with the hydrophobic environment of G4 DNA, resulting in greater motional restriction, longer fluorescence lifetime, and higher rotational correlation time compared to naringenin. These findings underscore the importance of molecular planarity in selective G4 DNA recognition and provide valuable insights for designing flavonoid-based anticancer agents targeting G4 structures.

The study seeks to provide insights for designing selective G4 DNA binders based on flavonoid scaffolds, which are potential targets for anticancer drug development.

- How does the planarity of the C-ring in flavonoid structures affect their interaction with G4 DNA?

- Can the findings on flavonoid-DNA binding be generalized to other chemical classes with similar scaffolds?

Despite possessing quite similar structural backbones, fisetin exhibits preferential interaction with G4 DNA in comparison to the duplex, while the reverse occurs for naringenin. Molecular modeling studies clearly demonstrate that the spatial structures of the flavonoids may cause these differences in the G4 binding. The more coplanar conformation of fisetin may be responsible for the strong binding of this flavonol with the G4. However, due to the absence of a C2-C3 double bond in the C-ring, naringenin adopts a significant noncoplanar conformation relative to the ring A/C plane, resulting in a poor binding with the G4 structure. Interestingly, fisetin forms a greater number of H-bonds with G4 than that of naringenin which may also lead to the higher affinity of fisetin toward G4 than naringenin. This study also exemplifies the application of dual emission behavior of flavonoids to probe selective G4 DNA recognition and lays the basis for further applications in this direction. To the best of our knowledge, this may be the first report of two closely similar structured flavonoid molecules showing sharply contrasting selectivity for binding with different DNA structures. dataset_item.question: How do ammonia, organotins, and phosphate contribute to growth inhibition of Heterocypris incongruens in sediments?
dataset_item.answer:
Ammonia (NH₃) and organotins, particularly tributyltin (TBT⁺), are the primary contributors to the growth inhibition of *Heterocypris incongruens* in sediments, each exhibiting a toxicity unit (TU) of 0.3. These compounds act as direct inhibitors of growth, with organotins showing strong correlation to toxicity despite their relatively low initial TU contribution. In contrast, phosphate (HPO₄²⁻) has a growth-promoting effect, reducing the toxic impact with a TU of -0.3. 

Speciation calculations indicate that ammonia, organotins, and phosphate collectively account for up to 90% of the observed variance in growth inhibition across various water bodies. Regional differences in toxicity are evident, with sediments in West Flanders demonstrating higher toxic pressure compared to inland areas. The mechanism involves ammonia and organotins exerting toxic effects, while phosphate mitigates their impact by promoting growth. These findings underscore the importance of balancing nutrient levels and controlling toxic compounds in sediment management strategies.

dataset_item.question: How does modularity maximization influence the design and performance of distributed model predictive control in amine gas sweetening plants?
dataset_item.answer: Modularity maximization in distributed model predictive control (DMPC) for amine gas sweetening plants optimizes the decomposition of the plant into subnetworks, typically separating the absorption and regeneration stages. This optimal decomposition results in a control architecture that achieves closed-loop performance comparable to centralized model predictive control (CMPC) while outperforming decentralized and suboptimal distributed MPC strategies. By leveraging modularity, the DMPC framework ensures robust disturbance rejection and noise tolerance, critical for tightly integrated large-scale plants. Furthermore, the computational efficiency of this modular approach makes it highly practical for real-time applications, striking an effective balance between control precision and scalability.

The paper aims to develop and evaluate a distributed model predictive control (DMPC) strategy for optimizing the plant-wide control of an amine gas sweetening plant. The process involves removing sour gases (hydrogen sulfide and carbon dioxide) from natural gas using monoethanolamine absorption. The study introduces a modularity-based plant decomposition algorithm for distributed control and compares the performance and computational efficiency of distributed, decentralized, and centralized control approaches.

---

### 2. Classification of Purpose:
The purpose emphasizes **"<method>"**, as the focus is on the development and application of a modularity-based decomposition algorithm and the evaluation of control strategies.

- How does the modularity-based decomposition algorithm improve the efficiency of distributed model predictive control in amine gas sweetening plants?

- How does the use of monoethanolamine absorption impact the control dynamics and optimization challenges in the removal of sour gases?
- What are the critical factors in designing distributed control systems for plant-wide operations in gas sweetening processes?
- Can the proposed DMPC approach be generalized to other chemical processing plants or distributed parameter systems?

The optimal architecture for DMPC was obtained from a modularity maximization algorithm which separates the two stages of absorption and regeneration as different subnetworks. The performance of DMPC on the optimal decomposition was compared with that of a fully centralized MPC architecture, a decentralized MPC architecture, and distributed MPC on the suboptimal decomposition obtained from the modularity maximization algorithm. The closed-loop performance of DMPC implemented on the optimal decomposition was found to be comparable to that of CMPC and superior to the other architectures for all the control problems considered. The computation time for solving the optimization problem was also reasonably low (larger than only the decentralized MPC architecture) for DMPC based on the optimal decomposition. This work, thus, demonstrates a promising path for designing practically implementable model based controllers for large-scale tightly integrated plants. Future research will address the state estimation problem, further improvement and validation of the model based on plant data, and the real-time implementation of the proposed control structure.

The modularity maximization algorithm used in the study of distributed model predictive control (DMPC) in an amine gas sweetening plant influenced the design and performance of the control system in several ways:

1.  **Optimal Architecture**: The modularity maximization algorithm separated the two stages of absorption and regeneration as different subnetworks, which led to an optimal architecture for the DMPC. This separation improved the performance of the control system by reducing the complexity and increasing the scalability of the model.
2.  **Improved Performance**: The DMPC implemented on the optimal decomposition achieved comparable performance to the centralized MPC (CMPC) and superior performance to the decentralized MPC and distributed MPC on the suboptimal decomposition.

However, there are some limitations and challenges associated with the use of modularity maximization in DMPC, such as:

1.  **Optimization Problem**: The optimization problem becomes increasingly complex as the number of subnetworks increases, which can lead to high computational costs and reduced accuracy.
2.  **Communication and Coordination**: The modularity maximization algorithm requires effective communication and coordination between the subnetworks, which can be challenging in a distributed control system.

To address these challenges, future research should focus on:

1.  **Improving the Optimization Problem**: Developing more efficient optimization algorithms or techniques to reduce the computational costs and improve the accuracy of the solution.
2.  **Enhancing Communication and Coordination**: Developing more efficient communication and coordination protocols to ensure seamless interaction between the subnetworks.
3.  **Stability and Robustness**: Investigating the stability and robustness of the closed-loop system with the proposed DMPC architecture and the proposed estimator.

However, further research is needed to overcome the challenges associated with the use of modularity maximization in DMPC and to improve the scalability and robustness of the control system.

dataset_item.question: How can criteria be developed to select fate and transport models for estimating eutrophication-related impacts in life cycle assessment?
dataset_item.answer:
Criteria for selecting fate and transport (F&T) models for estimating eutrophication-related impacts in life cycle assessment (LCA) can be developed by integrating scientific rigor with practical constraints. The selection process involves identifying candidate models through systematic literature searches, focusing on models published between 2007 and 2017, actively maintained, and widely used—particularly by reputable organizations such as the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). 

Key criteria include:
1. **Model Maintenance and Usage**: Prioritize models that are actively updated, widely applied, and endorsed by recognized agencies (e.g., EPA) to ensure reliability and relevance.
2. **Geographic and Temporal Scope**: Assess the geographic coverage, spatial resolution, and time step of the models to ensure compatibility with the study’s context and objectives.
3. **Representation of Nutrient Dynamics**: Evaluate the model’s ability to accurately represent nutrient loading sources, transport mechanisms, removal processes, and transformation pathways critical to eutrophication modeling.
4. **Accessibility**: Favor publicly available models to facilitate transparency and reproducibility in research.
5. **Practical Constraints**: Consider limitations such as site specificity and challenges in spatial-temporal distribution to balance scientific rigor with feasibility.
6. **Structured Evaluation**: Use a rubric or spreadsheet to systematically assess model suitability based on metadata (e.g., geographic scope, spatial resolution) and nutrient-specific factors (e.g., nitrogen and phosphorus cycling processes).

The goal is to select models that effectively capture nutrient input, transport, removal, and transformation processes while accommodating practical challenges such as resolution limitations and site-specific variability. This ensures the selected models are scientifically robust, contextually relevant, and accessible for eutrophication-related LCA applications.

dataset_item.question: What is the effect of Li and Cl atomic dopants on the band gaps and electronic structure of polythiophene and polypyrrole polymers?
dataset_item.answer:
Li and Cl atomic dopants significantly alter the electronic structure and band gaps of polythiophene (PTh) and polypyrrole (PPy) polymers, as confirmed by density functional theory (DFT) calculations. Lithium acts as an n-type dopant, causing an upward shift in the Fermi level, while chlorine functions as a p-type dopant, resulting in a downward shift in the Fermi level. Both dopants effectively reduce the HOMO-LUMO gap of these polymers, with a pronounced effect observed in polythiophene and its analogs, where sulfur is replaced by oxygen, selenium, or tellurium, and in polypyrrole analogs, where nitrogen is substituted with phosphorus, arsenic, or antimony.

Structural changes in the polymer chains are induced upon doping, facilitating charge transfer between the dopants and the polymers, as supported by Mulliken population analysis. These electronic modifications enhance the tunability of polythiophene and polypyrrole for various electronic device applications, including semiconductors and optoelectronic devices.

dataset_item.question: What is the difference in the excited-state proton transfer mechanism between 2,6-diazaindole clusters containing three and four water molecules?
dataset_item.answer:
The excited-state proton transfer (ESPT) mechanism in 2,6-diazaindole (2,6-DAI) clusters depends on the number of water molecules due to differences in hydrogen bonding configurations and reaction pathways. For the 2,6-DAI (H₂O)₃ cluster, ESPT follows a type A process, while for the 2,6-DAI (H₂O)₄ cluster, ESPT occurs via a type C process. The transition to a type C mechanism in the four-water cluster is driven by the enhanced stability of the proton-transferred (PT) form due to optimized hydrogen bonding interactions. 

Despite the distinct pathways, both clusters exhibit nearly identical energy barriers in the S₁ state, with type A having an energy barrier of 13.16 kcal/mol and type C having an energy barrier of 13.14 kcal/mol. Frontier molecular orbital analysis confirms charge redistribution during ESPT, facilitated by enhanced hydrogen bonding in the excited state. These findings demonstrate that 2,6-DAI can engage in ESPT through either three- or four-water-molecule clusters, following energetically similar but mechanistically distinct pathways.

dataset_item.question: How does the hidden Markov model method compare to the hindered Brownian diffusion method in simulating continuous-wave electron paramagnetic resonance spectra of spin-labeled proteins?
dataset_item.answer:
The hidden Markov model (HMM) method is superior to the hindered Brownian diffusion (HBD) method for simulating continuous-wave electron paramagnetic resonance (CW EPR) spectra of spin-labeled proteins. HMM excels at capturing multi-scale and jump-like transitions between spin-label orientations, making it highly effective for systems with restricted dynamics, such as TOAC-polyalanine, as well as faster, more mobile dynamics observed in R1-labeled proteins. In contrast, HBD relies on a single rotational diffusion tensor and orientational potential energy, which limits its ability to accurately model restricted multisite dynamics and complex motions.

Additionally, HMM offers significant computational advantages, being approximately 50 times faster than HBD for simulating faster dynamics. This efficiency is achieved by avoiding the computational bottleneck associated with interpolative evaluation of the torque term in HBD at each time step. Overall, HMM provides greater flexibility, accuracy, and performance across different spin-label dynamics, making it the preferred method for CW EPR spectral simulations.

dataset_item.question: What are the effects of ultrasound on dispersion and flow behavior in micropacked-bed reactors?
dataset_item.answer: High-power, low-frequency (∼40 kHz) ultrasound significantly enhances dispersion and flow behavior in micropacked-bed reactors by reducing liquid dispersion by two orders of magnitude and promoting near-plug-flow operation. This improvement is achieved through partial fluidization of the packed bed, which dynamically disrupts gas channeling, disperses the gas phase uniformly, and enhances phase homogenization, even at high flow rates. Visualization and residence time distribution experiments confirm these effects, demonstrating the stabilization of flow and reduction of channeling. Additionally, ultrasound continuously modifies gas channels, thereby mitigating liquid dispersion and ensuring more uniform flow. While these findings highlight the potential of ultrasound to improve microscale reactor performance, further studies are needed to optimize reactor design, assess mass transfer contributions, and address potential catalyst damage from cavitation.

dataset_item.question: How does ionic strength influence the twisting period and stability of charged amphiphile nanoribbons?
dataset_item.answer: Ionic strength influences the twisting period and stability of charged amphiphile nanoribbons by modulating electrostatic interactions. At low ionic strengths, reduced electrostatic screening enhances edge charge stabilization, favoring larger twisting periods and promoting helicoid stability. Twisting redistributes charges toward the edges, lowering the system's free energy, making the helicoid shape energetically favorable. However, as ionic strength increases, salt ions screen electrostatic interactions, reducing the electrostatic benefit of twisting and destabilizing the helicoid shape. This leads to shorter twisting periods and flatter ribbons, especially for flexible nanoribbons with high surface charge densities. While molecular chirality can independently drive twisting, electrostatic effects significantly modulate the optimal twisting period, as observed experimentally.

dataset_item.question: How does the use of one-electron pseudopotential calculations combined with advanced computational techniques affect the modeling of the Mg+He van der Waals system?
dataset_item.answer:
The use of one-electron pseudopotential calculations, combined with advanced computational techniques, significantly enhances the modeling of the Mg+He van der Waals system by simplifying the complex problem to a single valence electron while retaining high accuracy. This approach employs semilocal pseudopotentials to describe interactions between the Mg²⁺ core and the valence electron with helium, and high-level CCSD(T) calculations to accurately account for core-core interactions. Large Gaussian basis sets are utilized to improve the precision of the results, while the Tang-Toennies analytical expression refines the potential energy surfaces at intermediate distances. Spin-orbit coupling effects are incorporated using a semiempirical method, leading to energy splitting and minor shifts in equilibrium distances.

The derived potential energy surfaces and spectroscopic constants for the X²Σ⁺ and A²Π states are consistent with prior studies, validating the accuracy of the approach. These results provide a robust foundation for future investigations into Mg+He clusters, helium nanodroplet interactions, and spectral broadening effects in He gas collisions. The combined use of pseudopotential calculations and advanced computational methods ensures a detailed and reliable description of the Mg+He van der Waals system across both ground and excited states.

dataset_item.question: How does the use of HF during synthesis influence the crystallinity and phase formation of zirconium coordination polymers prepared with benzenephosphonate derivatives?
dataset_item.answer: The use of hydrofluoric acid (HF) as a mineralizer during the synthesis of zirconium coordination polymers with benzenephosphonate derivatives promotes crystallinity but results in mixed-phase compounds with unresolved structures. In contrast, fluoride-free synthesis produces poorly crystalline zirconium benzenetriphosphonates (ZrBTP-x) that exhibit superior extraction performance for trivalent lanthanides and tetravalent thorium under highly acidic conditions (>3 M HNO₃). These fluoride-free materials demonstrate fast extraction kinetics, high selectivity for heavy lanthanides, and thermal stability. Upon heating, they form highly crystalline pyrophosphates (AIVP₂O₇), which are suitable for radioactive waste disposal. Therefore, while HF enhances crystallinity, it compromises phase purity and extraction efficiency, making fluoride-free synthesis more advantageous for applications requiring superior extraction performance and selectivity.

It is worth noting that the use of HF as a mineralizer can be useful in certain cases, such as the preparation of crystalline materials with specific properties, but it may not be the best choice for all applications. In some cases, the absence of HF or the use of alternative mineralizers may be preferred to achieve the desired material properties.

dataset_item.question: What is the impact of truncation of C-terminal regions on structural stability and interaction dynamics of pyruvate dehydrogenase complex subunits E2 and E3BP?
dataset_item.answer: Truncation of the C-terminal regions in pyruvate dehydrogenase complex subunits E2 and E3BP significantly destabilizes their structural stability and interaction dynamics. Molecular dynamics simulations reveal that while wild-type (WT) E2 and E3BP dimers maintain stable orientations with tightly bound C-terminals embedded in hydrophobic pockets, truncated versions (E2-t8 and E3BP-t7) rapidly lose mutual alignment and detach from these binding pockets. This detachment is accompanied by a sharp reduction in hydrophobic interactions, which play a dominant role in dimer stability and core assembly integrity. The increased distances between C-terminal regions and hydrophobic pockets further underscore the loss of structural cohesion upon truncation. These findings align with experimental observations in other pyruvate dehydrogenase complex species and provide molecular-level evidence for human PDC assembly mechanisms. Preliminary experimental data corroborate these results, demonstrating core disassembly upon truncation. These insights enhance the understanding of human PDC assembly and stability, while informing future designs of artificial multienzyme systems.

dataset_item.question: What are the advantages of oxidative coupling reactions for bioconjugation in terms of reaction rate, selectivity, and product stability?
dataset_item.answer: Oxidative coupling reactions for bioconjugation offer several advantages that make them highly effective for diverse applications. They exhibit rapid reaction rates, typically completing in 2–20 minutes even at micromolar concentrations, which is ideal for time-sensitive processes like radiolabeling and minimizes biomolecule denaturation. These reactions are minimally affected by steric hindrance, enabling efficient coupling of sterically hindered or full-sized biomolecules. The resulting conjugates are highly stable, showing strong resistance to hydrolysis, reducing agents, oxidants, and nucleophiles, ensuring long-term product integrity. Additionally, these methods utilize readily available, water-soluble functional groups and employ easily removable oxidants, simplifying purification. High selectivity is achieved for both natural and unnatural functional groups by fine-tuning reaction conditions or reactant structures, offering versatility and an expanded substrate scope. The inherent compatibility with electron-rich aromatic systems further underscores the potential for discovering novel transformations, making oxidative coupling a powerful tool for bioconjugation and biomolecular material synthesis.

dataset_item.question: What structural differences arise between zirconium oxide prepared by oxidation of zirconium predeposited on copper versus direct deposition of zirconium under oxygen ambient?
dataset_item.answer:
Structural differences between zirconium oxide (ZrO₂) prepared by oxidation of zirconium predeposited on copper versus direct deposition of zirconium under oxygen ambient arise from variations in oxidation pathways, interfacial interactions, and growth modes. 

When zirconium is vapor-deposited on copper at room temperature (300K) followed by oxidation at elevated temperatures (600K), the resulting ZrO₂ forms well-defined, stable islands with larger and more isolated structures. This growth mode is attributed to the controlled oxidation process that minimizes interactions with the underlying copper substrate. Scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) confirms the formation of these distinct ZrO₂ islands, while X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) shows the presence of stoichiometric ZrO₂ with fewer oxygen deficiencies.

In contrast, direct deposition of zirconium in an oxygen ambient on preoxidized CuOₓ/Cu(111) at 600K leads to less uniform ZrO₂ structures and stronger interfacial interactions with the CuOₓ support. STM reveals smaller and less isolated islands, while XPS indicates the initial formation of oxygen-deficient ZrOₓ phases, requiring further oxidation to achieve stoichiometric ZrO₂. The differences in structure and composition stem from the direct exposure of zirconium to oxygen during deposition and the influence of the preoxidized copper substrate on the oxidation process.

Overall, the predeposition and subsequent oxidation approach produces more stable and well-defined ZrO₂ structures, while direct deposition under oxygen ambient results in less uniform growth and oxygen-deficient phases due to differing oxidation dynamics and substrate interactions.

dataset_item.question: How does confinement in nanopores affect nanoscale segregation and packing of hydrophobic ionic liquids?
dataset_item.answer: Confinement within nanopores significantly impacts the nanoscale segregation and packing of hydrophobic ionic liquids, such as [C6mim][PF6]. Depending on the ionic liquid-to-precursor ratio, three distinct nanopore morphologies—H2, H3, and H4—are observed. Narrow H2 and H4 nanopores disrupt the intrinsic nanoscale segregation of the ionic liquid due to spatial constraints, while broader H3 nanopores preserve this segregation despite rough surface topography. Within H3 nanopores, the confined ionic liquid exhibits tighter packing, with characteristic lengths reduced to 1.55–1.65 nm compared to the bulk value of 1.71 nm. This enhanced packing is driven by repulsive interactions between the [PF6]⁻ anions and silanol groups on the silica surface. These morphological transitions are governed by the minimization of interfacial energy and the maximization of entropy, which together determine the balance between segregation preservation and packing behavior in confinement.

   The study has implications for applications where hydrophobic ionic liquids are confined in nanopores, such as in the development of solid-state electrolytes, fuel cells, and other energy storage devices. Understanding the effect of confinement on nanoscale segregation and packing of hydrophobic ionic liquids can help in designing materials with optimized properties.

dataset_item.question: What are the benefits of decomposing probabilistic graphical models into hierarchical structures for process monitoring?
dataset_item.answer: Decomposing probabilistic graphical models into hierarchical structures offers significant benefits for process monitoring by leveraging conditional dependencies among process variables. This hierarchical decomposition enables the efficient representation of the joint probability distribution as a product of conditional densities and low-dimensional densities, simplifying the estimation process. By utilizing nonparametric kernel density estimation, this approach becomes distribution-free, making it particularly effective for handling nonlinear and non-Gaussian systems. Compared to traditional methods like PCA-based contribution plots, hierarchical decomposition improves fault detection and isolation by pinpointing faulty variables with greater accuracy. This capability has been demonstrated in applications such as blast furnace iron-making processes, where it enhances fault localization and process monitoring efficiency.

dataset_item.question: How does the deposition method of sodium fluoride affect the interfacial dipole on organic layers like P3HT and PCBM?
dataset_item.answer: The deposition method of sodium fluoride (NaF) plays a crucial role in determining the interfacial dipole on organic layers like P3HT and PCBM. Sequential depositions, compared to single thick depositions, lead to distinct dipole changes due to variations in interfacial dipole formation and potential water trapping. For NaF/P3HT, the outward-facing dipole component becomes more positive, while for NaF/PCBM, it becomes less positive. These dipole changes are attributed to the electronic structure modifications at the interface, influenced by the deposition method. Thick NaF layers can cause fluorination and damage to the conjugated π states of PCBM, degrading device performance, whereas thin layers enhance charge injection due to favorable dipole effects. Furthermore, the island-like growth mechanism of NaF, similar to LiF, contributes to the interfacial property changes. Understanding these effects is critical for optimizing charge injection and improving the performance of organic photovoltaic devices.

dataset_item.question: How does molecular shape, particularly rigidity of ring structures, influence diffusion rates of hydrocarbons in activated carbon?
dataset_item.answer:
The molecular shape, particularly the rigidity of ring structures, plays a significant role in influencing the diffusion rates of hydrocarbons in activated carbon. Rigid ring structures hinder molecular mobility, resulting in slower diffusion compared to flexible, linear hydrocarbons. Experimental studies using concentration-swing frequency response (CSFR) measurements on C10 hydrocarbons in BPL activated carbon have shown that rigid molecules, such as α-pinene and decalin, diffuse more slowly than flexible molecules like n-decane. This trend was observed across diffusion coefficients ranging from approximately 1 × 10⁻¹² m²/s in the Henry's law regime to higher values at elevated concentrations.

The impact of molecular rigidity on diffusion rates is supported by quantitative structure-activity relationship (QSAR) analysis, which highlights molecular shape factors as key determinants of diffusivity. The absence of size exclusion effects in the porous structure of BPL activated carbon further confirms that molecular rigidity, rather than size, is the dominant factor affecting diffusion. The order of diffusion rates observed—n-decane > limonene > perfluorodecalin > decalin > α-pinene—illustrates how increased ring rigidity reduces mobility within the activated carbon's porous framework. In conclusion, hydrocarbons with rigid ring structures experience slower diffusion due to restricted molecular motion within the pores.

dataset_item.question: How does functionalized graphene improve matrix strength of silicone rubber compared to chemically reduced graphene?
dataset_item.answer: Functionalized graphene (FG) significantly improves the matrix strength of silicone rubber (VMQ) compared to chemically reduced graphene (rGO), due to its stronger compatibility and interactions with the polymer matrix. Rheological tests demonstrate that FG enhances matrix strength by approximately six times, whereas rGO achieves only a two-fold increase. This superior matrix reinforcement by FG prevents cell wall shrinkage during foaming, resulting in VMQ/FG foams with larger cell sizes and lower density—one-third that of VMQ/rGO foams at 1 wt% loading. Additionally, FG-reinforced foams exhibit superior mechanical properties, including higher specific compression strength (1.21 MPa·cm³/g vs. 0.85 MPa·cm³/g for VMQ/rGO), better deformation recovery (2% permanent compression set with full recovery in less than 0.5 hours), and enhanced tensile strength (130%) and elongation at break (140%) compared to VMQ/rGO foams. These properties make FG-reinforced foams highly suitable for demanding high- and low-temperature applications.

dataset_item.question: How can reduced-order modeling improve the efficiency of Bayesian parameter inference for stochastic gene expression models?
dataset_item.answer: Reduced-order modeling enhances the efficiency of Bayesian parameter inference for stochastic gene expression models by simplifying computational complexity and accelerating the sampling process, while maintaining high accuracy in parameter estimation and uncertainty quantification. This is achieved through methods such as adaptive delayed acceptance Metropolis-Hastings (ADAMH) and hybrid extensions, which leverage adaptive tuning of proposal distributions and reduced-order approximations. These approaches reduce computational costs compared to traditional finite state projection (FSP) methods, enabling faster and more scalable inference from single-cell data, including smFISH, time-lapse microscopy, and single-cell sequencing. Numerical tests confirm that reduced-order models preserve precision while delivering substantial speedups, making them particularly effective for analyzing complex stochastic processes in single-cell gene expression studies.

Reduced-order modeling can improve the efficiency of Bayesian parameter inference for stochastic gene expression models in several ways:

1.  **Model Simplification**: Reduced-order modeling reduces the complexity of the original model by eliminating non-essential components and simplifying the mathematical formulation. This simplification can significantly reduce the computational cost of Bayesian inference, making it feasible to analyze large and complex gene expression models.
2.  **Dimensionality Reduction**: Reduced-order modeling can also be used to reduce the dimensionality of the parameter space, which can help to avoid overfitting and improve the convergence of Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithms used in Bayesian inference.
3.  **Faster Sampling**: By reducing the complexity of the model and the dimensionality of the parameter space, reduced-order modeling can lead to faster sampling times in MCMC algorithms, allowing for more efficient exploration of the parameter space and better estimation of posterior distributions.
4.  **Improved Accuracy**: Reduced-order modeling can also improve the accuracy of Bayesian inference by reducing the impact of model errors and approximations on the posterior distribution. By eliminating non-essential components and simplifying the model, reduced-order modeling can provide a more accurate representation of the underlying system.
5.  **Scalability**: Reduced-order modeling can make Bayesian inference more scalable, allowing for the analysis of larger and more complex gene expression models that were previously intractable.

To implement reduced-order modeling in Bayesian parameter inference for stochastic gene expression models, you can follow these steps:

1.  **Identify the key components**: Identify the essential components of the model that contribute most to the behavior of the system. These components may include specific genes, proteins, or biochemical reactions.
2.  **Simplify the model**: Simplify the original model by eliminating non-essential components and reducing the dimensionality of the parameter space.
3.  **Develop a reduced-order model**: Develop a reduced-order model that captures the essential behavior of the original system. This may involve using techniques such as principal component analysis (PCA), singular value decomposition (SVD), or other dimensionality reduction methods.
4.  **Perform Bayesian inference**: Perform Bayesian inference on the reduced-order model using MCMC algorithms or other methods. This will provide a posterior distribution over the reduced parameter space.
5.  **Map back to the original parameter space**: Map the posterior distribution back to the original parameter space to obtain the desired estimates of model parameters.

By following these steps, reduced-order modeling can significantly improve the efficiency and accuracy of Bayesian parameter inference for stochastic gene expression models.

dataset_item.question: How does the length of the alkyl tail on imidazolium cations influence density turnover and nanostructuring in ionic liquid and water binary mixtures?
dataset_item.answer:
The length of the alkyl tail on imidazolium cations plays a crucial role in determining density turnover and nanostructuring in ionic liquid (IL)/water binary mixtures. At lower water concentrations, density increases due to enhanced polar domain structuring involving cation headgroups, anions, and water molecules. This structuring peaks at a specific water mole fraction, which depends on the alkyl tail length. For shorter-tailed cations, such as ethyl-methyl imidazolium ([emim][Ac]), the density turnover occurs at a water mole fraction (Xw) of approximately 0.5, driven by maximal polar domain structuring. As water content increases, further disruption of hydrogen-bonded anion bridges causes density to decline.

For longer-tailed cations, such as butyl-methyl ([bmim][Ac]) and hexyl-methyl imidazolium ([hmim][Ac]), the density turnover is delayed to higher water mole fractions (Xw > 0.7). This delay is attributed to water-induced aggregation of hydrophobic alkyl tails, which enhances nanostructuring even as polar domain correlations weaken. The longer tails provide greater hydrophobicity, promoting tail aggregation and sustaining nanostructuring at higher water concentrations. Thus, alkyl tail length influences the water mole fraction at which density turnover occurs by modulating the balance between polar domain structuring and hydrophobic tail aggregation.

inference_contexts: In this study, we have primarily focused on the effect of the imidazolium cation tail length on the nanostructural reorganization and dynamics of [R n mim] [Ac]/water binary mixtures, and their consequent influence on the anomalous densities of this IL family. We observed that the density change exhibited by different ILs of this family could be clearly demarcated into two regimes (Figure ). While the increased structuring among the polar components (cation headgroup, anion, and water) led to the initial rise in density in the first regime (X w ≤ 0.5), the role of the alkyl tail became evident in the second regime of higher water concentrations. As a result, the density of [emim] [Ac]/water binary mixtures showed a turnover at X w = 0.5, whereas, for longer-tailed [bmim] and [hmim] cations, the turnover was shifted to X w > 0.7 (see Figures , , and ). As evident from Figures and , the spatial correlation in the polar domain maximizes at X w = 0.5, beyond which the nanostructuring continues to grow only in cations with longer alkyl chains due to water-induced tail aggregation (Figures - and Figures S4-S6, Supporting Information). This differential nanostructuring caused by varying cation tail lengths could explain the different turnover points in the measured densities of [emim] [Ac]/water and [bmim] [Ac]/water binary mixtures. ,

Acetate anion-water interactions were found to play a key role in structuring the polar domain of the binary mixtures in agreement with earlier studies. , An in-depth analysis showed that the pattern of these interactions changed with water concentration, which intricately controlled not only the initial rise but also the subsequent turnover in density of [R n mim] [Ac]/water binary mixtures. When present in low concentrations, isolated water molecules occupy locations between adjacent anions and form water-mediated hydrogen bonded anion bridges (Figure a). As more and more hydrogen bonded bridges are formed (Table ), the spatial correlation among the IL anions (and consequently among the cation head groups) increases, leading to a steady rise in density up to X w ~ 0.5. Upon further dilution, the incoming water disrupts the water-mediated anion bridges and increasingly forms bifurcated anion-water hydrogen bonds, leading to decreased anion structuring and a decline in the density. However, this density turnover is shifted to higher concentration in longer-tailed cations, due to water-induced tail aggregation, as described above. The dynamics of these mixtures also exhibited a similar turnover at moderate water concentration.

MD simulations of three imidazolium-based LTILs were carried out using a nonpolarizable all-atom force field, which is a refined version of the CL&P force field. The effects of temperature and alkyl chain length on the densities, MSDs, self-diffusivities, viscosities, electrical conductivities, transference numbers, and hydrodynamic radii of the cations and anions of the studied LTILs were investigated. The calculated densities of the LTILs are greater than those of both MILs and DILs and decrease with increasing temperature and alkyl chain length between the imidazolium rings. Detailed microscopic structures of the studied LTILs were discussed in terms of RDFs and SDFs. The results show that, similar to that in MILs and DILs, the anions are very well organized around the cationic rings and tend to spend most of their time around the ring compared with alkyl chain atoms. Diffusion coefficients of the studied LTILs are smaller than those of both MILs and DILs, with comparable viscosities. It can be observed that, unlike those of MILs and DILs, the diffusion coefficients of the cations and anions of the studied LTILs increase with increasing length of the alkyl chain between the rings from LTIL-1 to LTIL-2 but decrease for LTIL-3, which is in a good agreement with the trend of viscosity data. The calculated MSDs and diffusion coefficients of the alkyl chain, middle ring, and side ring in each of the studied LTILs are similar, which indicates that the motion of these groups is highly correlated to each other. The trend of the molar electrical conductivity of the studied LTILs is in contrast to the viscosity values of these ILs. LTIL-2, which has the lowest viscosity, has a greater molar electrical conductivity. The large transference numbers of the cations (0.77 < t + < 0.81) show that, similar to that in MILs and DILs, cations have a major contribution to electric current, and this contribution is more than that in both MILs and DILs.

As a first report on the SAXS mearements for the imidazolium-based ILs at ambient pressure, Triolo et al. showed that a characteristic peak at the low-Q region (2-4 nm-1) appeared. They proposed that this characteristic prepeak is direct evidence of the structural heterogeneity (nanophase separation) of ILs and the value of Bragg spacing D is the measure of an average size of the domain (the alkyl tail domain size + the thickness of the surrounding charged shell). However, there have been some debates on the molecular origin of the low-Q peak, and the relationship between liquid structure and the low-Q peak. For example, it was suggested that the position of the prepeak corresponds to a spatial correlation length, such as the distance between neighboring shells in the liquid structure and/or intermolecular correlations between anion pairs, adjacent tails, and cation tail/anion pairs.
